#10424. Pixel Tag is a brilliant Band-Aid on a Find Hub network Google can’t easily fix

The Google Pixel Tag is here and, at least so far, it’s really good. But fresh hardware and some new features can’t fix the core problem. Google’s Find Hub network has been restricted from the very start, and it’s not something Google can easily fix.

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every Sunday along with ‘Inbox’ on Tuesday and Thursday. You can find past issues here.

The good news on Pixel Tag: this is a well-built tracker that, unlike others, is the clear product of the hardware having direct access to the software. Little touches like being able to adjust ringer volume on the fly combine nicely with UWB – the latter something we rarely see on third-party devices largely due to Apple – all things that elevate the Find Hub tracker to what we called the new “gold standard.”

The bad news: this is still a Find Hub tracker.

Google’s Find Hub network has improved dramatically over the two years since its launch. Where Google originally had to admit that tracking performance was lacking (a nice way of putting it, frankly), improvements started arriving in 2025. We noticed that the network seemed to be working much better a few months after its wide rollout, and Google later confirmed speed improvements.

But, ultimately, the Find Hub network is still reeling from how it debuted.

Again, it’s gotten better since then, but it’s still not as good as it should be. Samsung’s network, limited solely to Galaxy phones, shouldn’t outperform Google’s. Find Hub trackers should be just as good as AirTags and the third-party trackers that work with Apple’s network. They’re just not, and I truly do believe it all boils down to this initial choice. One of the reasons this is getting better is that Google has been pushing users to the “all areas” setting during the setup of a new device – I’ve noticed this on some recent devices I set up, but it’s not been completely consistent just yet. That’s a good step forward but, even if it is the new default, that still requires millions of users to upgrade their devices, and we’ve never been in a better time to not upgrade your phone.

All of that is to say, the Pixel Tag isn’t fixing this problem. Surely, it’ll give Google some needed fire to fix the problem, but new hardware isn’t the solution. That’s something I was discussing with 9to5Google readers on our review. UWB is a tentpole feature of the Pixel Tag, but it doesn’t change the network problems, it just improves precision finding. We needed a first-party tracker like this regardless of the state of the network, something that really takes advantage of the platform and pushes it forward, but it’s just a quick fix, a Band-Aid.

What do you think? Have you found the Find Hub network reliable enough, or is there still room for improvement? Sound off in the comments below!

Intelligent Eyewear pre-orders are open now

Google’s other big product launch this week was Intelligent Eyewear, the first display-less Android XR glasses. Built in collaboration with Samsung, Warby Parker, and Gentle Monster, they’ve left a great first impression, and pricing starts at $395.

Google this week launched yet another new Gemini model, Hydrogen, which is a refresh of its Flash tier model and a “major standalone upgrade” on top of Gemini 3.8 Flash. Hydrogen is already powering AI features in Google Search.

Perhaps the biggest story in tech this week, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is out following not just an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, but two additional employee affairs beyond that were exposed.

Google this week rolled out the latest major Pixel update, based on Android 17 QPR2. It brings a bunch of new features to the lineup, primarily to the Pixel 10 series which added Rambler and other Pixel 11 features.

#10423. NowThis just bought one of Gen Z’s favorite Instagram news accounts. Here’s why

If Instagram is your preferred avenue for media consumption, you’ve probably come across posts by Impact. The popular Gen-Z-targeted account is characterized by its quick-turn analysis on progressive, left-wing topics ranging from identity politics to mental health and niche internet trends. That winning formula caught the attention of social video publisher NowThis, which recently acquired the brand.

Launched in 2020 by founders Tim Chau and Michelle Andrews, the Impact Instagram handle was born in the apex of Gen Z’s formative years, an era marked by a hyper-online generation who reckoned with Donald Trump, COVID-19, social isolation, canceled graduations, the murder of George Floyd, and climate disaster all in the same year. Impact created timely stories around narratives that Gen Z desperately craved and traditional media often failed to cover: Its content is often among the first to share pointed commentary on trending headlines. 

When comedian Shane Gillis was being criticized online for a misogynistic SNL bit, Impact published “Male comedians don’t actually have to hate women to be popular.” After the internet was in an uproar over the U.K. banning books authored by Sally Rooney due to her support for Palestine, Impact wrote about it immediately. Impact even creates content around shared woes that span multiple generations, helping it reach larger audiences—as seen in posts like “Is it rude to ask friends to stay with them when you visit their city?” The comments section of each post is the heart of the community the Impact team has built and a glimpse into real cultural capital, making it easy to see why NowThis chose to purchase the company. 

Founded in 2012 by former Huffington Post execs Kenneth Lerer and Eric Hippeau, NowThis began as a social-first go-to for millennial content before being acquired by Vox Media. As millennials aged into the next phase of adulthood, companies and news organizations from all corners of the internet competed for the coveted attention of young people, nudging the video publisher into a new chapter. In 2023, NowThis expanded into a large-scale media network targeting Gen Z, taking on a new CEO, Sharon Mussalli, and a new editor-in-chief, Michael Vito Valentino, while also reckoning with the ramifications of significant layoffs. This latest move in acquiring Impact—for an alleged seven-figure all-cash deal—demonstrates a commitment to reaching its target audience and the community of young people behind Impact. 

“[They] care about what’s happening in the world and want to understand how it connects to their relationships, their work, their culture, and their futures. That’s closely aligned with the Gen Z female audience we’re building for at NowThis. And we saw an opportunity to invest in that relationship and give it more room to grow,” Mussalli said in a statement via the NowThis PR team. 

She adds: “Impact brings a distinct editorial voice and a strong sense of what resonates with its community. We bring the production capabilities and experience developing original video franchises to help translate that into new series and recurring formats. Our ambition is to build something this audience can grow with, across all NowThis channels. That means giving people more than an individual story they encounter in their feed—it means creating recognizable programming they seek out, share, and return to.” 

In a statement to Fast Company, Chau, who is stepping down from the Impact staff but will remain involved in some capacity, calls the move “bittersweet.” “We put everything into Impact to get it where it is today, so stepping back isn’t easy. But we couldn’t be happier about where it’s headed, because we know NowThis is the right home for it. They’re leading in a space where social now dominates—really the first of their kind—and that’s exactly the future we want Impact to be part of.”

“My hope is that Impact stays the place young people go to for stories that actually land with them, the ones they talk about with friends, share, and sit with. Legacy media has struggled to resonate with this generation, and I hope Impact can keep being the place where they feel truly understood and connected,” Chau said.

#10420. A new report says free childcare in NYC will pay for itself

Since taking office, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has made it his mission to expand access to affordable childcare in the city, and for good reason. On average, NYC families spend $21,000 on childcare annually per child—equaling an estimated $10 billion citywide every year. While about 40% of children in the city receive some free or subsidized care, the remaining 60% receive none, leaving many families to pay entirely out of pocket.

A new report reveals how universal childcare would not only benefit families in New York City, but also boost the economy: Just 35 hours of free childcare per week could bring up to $6.5 billion in economic value each year, which would likely exceed the cost of providing that care. 

The report—which was produced by a nonpartisan think tank, the 5BORO Institute at Citizens Union, in partnership with Boston Consulting Group—surveyed more than 2,700 parents of children younger than 5, along with about a hundred families who moved away from New York City recently. 

According to the report, nearly 70% of children under the age of 6 are cared for by parents or adults who work. When those parents are unable to find care and forced to drop out of the workforce or switch jobs, the city loses $1.7 billion in annual income; among the parents surveyed, 15% altered their work situation due to childcare issues. For hourly workers, childcare gaps can force them to miss out on $360 million in earnings each year. The report also found that childcare was a leading concern for families who had left the city, a growing trend that is supported by plenty of other data. 

In other words, employers also feel the effects of inadequate access to care. That can mean high turnover or simply lost productivity if their workers regularly contend with disruptions to their childcare: More than half of the parents surveyed said they had missed at least one full day of work over the past three months, averaging three to four missed days.

These childcare gaps can cost New York City employers about 54 million hours of missed work, according to the report. The act of providing 35 hours of free childcare each week would also enable nearly 30,000 parents to reenter the workforce, which could yield more than a billion dollars in annual earnings.

Childcare has been a key focus for Mamdani since his campaign, and as Fast Company reported in a recent cover story, the mayor has even gotten the business community on board with its investments in this area. Mamdani is already building upon the universal 3-K program established by former Mayor Bill de Blasio to extend care to younger children; the recently launched 2-K program is now providing free, full-day childcare to 2,000 2-year-olds, with plans to serve an additional 10,000 children by next fall. (The city has provided free pre-K to all 4-year-olds since 2014.) 

Even business leaders who are critical of Mamdani have seemingly come around to the idea of free childcare, though they may not agree on how to achieve that. This fall, the 5BORO Institute created the NYC Child Care Business Council, bringing together a number of business leaders and organizations committed to putting their muscle behind this issue and advocating for childcare investment (something the business community has not historically done).

For years, employers have invested in generous parental leave policies and backup childcare benefits for their workforce to help them court top talent and retain some of their best employees. But it seems companies are finally realizing that their best efforts can’t make up for a lack of robust childcare options or offset the mounting cost of care.

“The market is not able to solve this problem,” Grace Rauh, the executive director of Citizens Union, recently told Fast Company. Citizens Union is a nonpartisan nonprofit founded in 1897 to promote government accountability, ethics, transparency, and civic engagement across New York. “Frankly, private businesses aren’t able to provide the kind of fully robust childcare benefits that their employees need,” Rauh said.

#10417. Nvidia’s first earnings call without Jensen Huang had one message: It’s business as usual

Nvidia on Tuesday held its first earnings call in its 33-year history without cofounder Jensen Huang, who resigned five days ago after a scandal involving an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy. After reporting strong third-quarter numbers, interim CEO Colette Kress (who has been Nvidia’s CFO since 2013) kept the call focused on Nvidia’s immediate business concerns. 

Analysts wanted to know what the company would say about the succession plan after Huang’s departure, and about the future of Nvidia’s pivotal role as the company powering the AI race. 

Most of the salient information about Huang was given at the front of the call by Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s chair of the board. Jones said Nvidia doesn’t intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO, providing a clapback to the growing contingent on social media lobbying for the ousted CEO’s return. Jones said the executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles is handling the search for a new CEO, but that Nvidia is looking at both internal and external candidates for the job. 

“The board is acting deliberately and in the best interest of the company’s employees and investors,” Jones said. “With that we will take no further questions about the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation.”

The numbers

Kress then took over the call and kept things focused on Nvidia’s numbers. Kress has run Nvidia’s earnings calls for years, but always alongside Huang, who set the company’s vision and did much of its dealmaking with customers and partners. Today her main job was to report the quarterly numbers, and convince investors that the world’s most important AI chip company can run without its founder.

The numbers, at least, are good. Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in revenue for its fiscal third quarter, well above Wall Street’s roughly $109 billion forecast, and projected $130 billion for the current quarter. Investors expected a beat. 

Kress said Nvidia has seen “explosive” adoption of its latest Vera Rubin computing platform, which includes a Rubin GPU and a Vera CPU. “Our momentum is real,” she said. “Our ambition will not change, our passion for innovation will not change.” 

Revenue for the quarter came in at $115.8 billion, about $6.5 billion higher than the roughly $109 billion analysts expected. Adjusted earnings were $2.68 per share, 21 cents above the $2.47 consensus. 

But all that happened during a third quarter that ended October 25—that is, before the Huang scandal broke. That’s why analysts were more concerned about the guidance numbers for a future without Huang. Some analysts had even questioned whether Nvidia would venture to give a full year 2028 guidance. 

But it did. For the short term, Nvidia forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion. The company had previously said it expects to see 70% growth in 2028, but Kress said its moving that guidance up to 75% growth, citing continued strong demand for AI infrastructure, including Vera Rubin, and despite the chance that chip exports to China will constrict somewhat in the wake of the Huang scandal.

That may have settled some analysts’ nerves about the AI sell-off that started in October, which was driven by the fear that Big Tech companies would slow their spending on AI data centers. 

Why this call mattered

Huang, who cofounded Nvidia in 1993, resigned on November 12 amid two scandals. The first involved an alleged affair with a woman U.S. intelligence believe may have been spying for China. Beijing has strongly denied the allegations. Nvidia’s board has opened an internal investigation into whether company or national security secrets were compromised. Huang stepped down shortly after reports of a second alleged affair, this one with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare (and the CEO’s direct report).

The board made Kress interim CEO. She also stays on as CFO until a permanent CEO is named. Longtime director Harvey Jones became Nvidia’s first board chair. 

The stock was already falling before the scandal. Nvidia closed at a record $239.24 on October 6. Shares then fell on fears that AI spending would slow, and fell further as the Huang story unfolded. By Tuesday the stock was below $154, its lowest level since mid-2025. That’s a loss of about $2 trillion in market value. That’s why Wall Street was listening to Kress so closely. 

Before the call, analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives predicted Kress would talk very little about Huang, that her main job would be to “restore order and give the Street confidence in the Nvidia story going forward,” he told Fox Business. 

And that’s exactly what happened. After the brief section at the front, the call had a business-as-usual tone, complete with a blizzard of numbers showing that Nvidia—as of the third quarter, at least—continues to sit at the center of the AI world.

#10416. What Breaks When a Self-Hosted LLM Gateway Hits 1,000 Concurrent Streams

We sent 1,000 streaming calls at the same moment through three self-hosted LLM gateways: the Langfuse AI Gateway, the LiteLLM proxy and AcruxCore. Each gateway was limited to 2 CPUs. As shipped, Langfuse finished 261 of the 1,000 streams and LiteLLM finished 403. Neither failure came from the gateway's own code.

Langfuse's failures came from Linux's open-file limit, which Docker sets to 1,024 by default. LiteLLM had that problem too, plus a second one: an empty key cache sent hundreds of database lookups at once, and the ones that waited longer than 10 seconds were rejected. This article shows how each failure looked, how we traced it to its cause, and the settings that fixed it.

This benchmark measured the resource consumption of three LLM gateways under scaling concurrent streaming loads.

Full latency, memory, and feature results are available in the Langfuse vs LiteLLM vs AcruxCore benchmark.

First-token times are medians of the streams that succeeded. Up to 250 streams, every gateway succeeded. Then the errors started, and they did not look alike:

A 502 and a 503 point at different layers, so we expected two different causes. Two of the three turned out to share one cause.

Linux counts every network connection as an open file, and it caps how many open files one process may hold. The cap has two values. The soft limit is the cap that is in force now. The hard limit is the ceiling: a process may raise its own soft limit up to that value, and no further.

A streaming gateway holds two connections for each stream: one from the client, and one to the model provider. That makes about 1,000 open files at 500 streams, and about 2,000 at 1,000 streams. A gateway also needs a few more files for its database, its logs and its own libraries.

Docker on our machine gave every container a soft limit of 1,024 and a hard limit of 524,288. All three gateways received the same two numbers. What differed was how each program treats them when it starts:

Node.js raises its own soft limit to the hard limit at startup. The Rust and Python services keep 1,024, and neither project's Compose file sets a higher value. So the two gateways ran out of open files near 500 streams, which is the point where the errors started.

The out-of-files error appeared as a failed connection, not as a clear message. The Langfuse gateway's logs showed failed connections to OpenAI, and also failed connections to Langfuse's own web service, which the gateway asks to check each key. Both come from one cause: a process that cannot open another file cannot open another socket. Its client then receives a 502.

Read the limit the process actually has, not the one you think Docker gave it. Process 1 is usually the main process in a container:

If the gateway runs under a supervisor or several workers, check each worker's process ID instead of process 1. To see how close a process is to its limit under load, count its open file descriptors:

Raise the limit for the gateway service in its Compose file. We used 65,536 for all three gateways:

The same ulimits block works on the LiteLLM service. On Kubernetes or another platform, check /proc//limits inside a running container rather than assuming a value.

With the open-file limit raised, the Langfuse gateway finished all 1,000 streams. LiteLLM still returned 503 errors. To separate the two causes, we ran LiteLLM with one worker and only the open-file limit raised. All 500 streams succeeded in that ladder, but 595 of 1,000 failed with 503.

The 503 message names the authentication database, so we read LiteLLM's logs and its source. The log gave the same reason for all 840 failed streams in these runs, 595 in that ladder and 245 in the cold-cache runs below:

When 500 calls arrive while the key is not in the cache, each call looks the key up in Postgres. All of those lookups queue for 10 connections. The worker was also using its whole CPU allowance at this point, which slows every query it sends and receives. We infer that this CPU load lengthens the queue, but we did not measure it separately. Whatever the share of each, the lookups at the back of the queue miss the 10-second deadline.

If that explanation is right, the failures should depend on whether the key is already in the cache. So we ran 500 streams four more times. Three runs started after 75 seconds with no calls, which is longer than the 60-second cache. One run started right after a single warm-up call:

The warm run had no failures. The cold runs failed by different amounts, 161, 84 and 0, because the result depends on how many lookups miss the deadline, and that changes from run to run. This probably explains why the earlier ladder succeeded at 500 and failed at 1,000. A run is a race between the lookup queue and the deadline, so a single ladder does not show where the limit is.

The warm-up result is the one we measured. Send one call with each virtual key after LiteLLM starts, and avoid quiet periods longer than 60 seconds before a traffic spike. A steady flow of traffic keeps the key in the cache.

LiteLLM also exposes three settings that act on this path. We did not test them, so treat them as places to look rather than proven fixes:

We raised the open-file limit to 65,536 for all three gateways and gave LiteLLM 2 workers, one per CPU, as its production guide recommends for a single machine. Then we ran the full ladder again:

The open-file errors were gone for every gateway, and the Langfuse gateway gave the fastest first token of the three. LiteLLM still returned 120 × 503 at 500. That level started about 60 seconds after the first call of the ladder, so the cached key had probably just expired. All 1,000 succeeded at the next level, which started within 60 seconds of the 500 level.

Once nothing failed, CPU decided the first-token times. LiteLLM used its whole 2-CPU allowance from 100 streams on, and its median first token took 19.2 seconds at 1,000 streams. AcruxCore also used both CPUs from 100 streams on, and its first token at 1,000 streams was 3.8 s at the median and 9.7 s at p95. The Langfuse gateway peaked at 1.65 CPUs and 168 MiB, with a first token of 1.7 s at the median and 9.6 s at p95.

Each gateway also needs the rest of its stack, and that stack uses CPU too. While the Langfuse gateway served 500 streams, its whole stack used up to 3.1 CPUs, because the web service checked keys and the worker and ClickHouse stored usage. AcruxCore's whole stack peaked at 4.0 CPUs, because its API writes a trace for every call to Postgres. Size the stack around the gateway, not only the gateway container.

Talha Anwar is a senior AI and full-stack engineer and writes about building and running AI systems at talhaanwar.com.

#10413. Why the smartest AI strategy starts with a little laziness

My employees know that I have an unconventional take on laziness: A lazy mindset doesn’t mean being unproductive. Often, it means finding a faster way to get something done. As Bill Gates famously said, “I choose a lazy person to do a hard job. Because a lazy person will find an easy way to do it.”

That’s why I encourage a lazy mindset, insofar as it means looking for more efficient ways to get things done—like leveraging the latest AI and automation tools. As I’ve seen in leading a company of more than 800 employees, people are eager to streamline their work. Studies confirm they’re doing it, whether their employers know about it or not.

One recent report found that while only 40% of companies surveyed had purchased official subscriptions to large language models, employees at more than 90% of those companies reported regular use of artificial intelligence. That often leads to piecemeal adoption and missed opportunities to realize AI’s full potential. Studies suggest AI can absorb 60% to 70% of busywork, freeing employees to focus on more meaningful tasks, like strategizing and coming up with innovative solutions.

Leaders should recognize this reality and adopt AI initiatives at the enterprise level. But the challenge isn’t finding opportunities—there are countless AI tools on the market, and more rolling out every day. It’s deciding which are worth pursuing. Every AI initiative comes with trade-offs, requiring time, budget, talent, and executive approval. Here are some tips for taking a more strategic approach to AI adoption in your company.

Start with business goals, not AI tools

Estimates of the number of AI tools on the market vary widely, from around 2,500 to more than 50,000. (If you look at live, available products, the lower figure is likely more accurate.) But one thing is indisputable: There are a ton, more than anyone could possibly test while working a full-time job. Amid this dizzying array of options, the first step in integrating AI into an organization is top down, clarifying your broader business goals.

Maybe your primary objective is to make it easier for users to incorporate your software into their everyday lives. AI-powered chatbots that field recurring user questions could be a wise investment. Or maybe your goal is to analyze users’ circumstances quickly and provide help faster. A tool that uses AI to analyze and synthesize vast amounts of data could transform your business. In healthcare, for example, IBM’s Watson has been used to analyze patient data and medical literature and provide doctors with evidence-based treatment options.

The key is to start with the problem you want to solve, not the technology you’re excited to use.

When leaders define their business goals, they can focus on AI opportunities that align with those goals and avoid the myriad distractions out there. Rather than dedicating resources to tools that merely speed things up, they can focus on uses with the greatest potential impact. They can deliberately pass on AI tools that don’t align with business objectives and concentrate their efforts where AI can make the biggest difference.

Let employees lead the way

If you were developing new cooking technology for a bakery, you probably wouldn’t begin with the product designer. You’d start by asking the baker how they work, where things tend to go awry, and how you might improve their processes. The best ideas for improving how people work often come from those on the front lines.

At my company, we invite all employees to share the AI tools they’ve discovered that have helped, or could potentially help, during our weekly demo days. It’s a valuable exchange of ideas—for example, customer service reps advising designers on how to better program help chatbots.

Experts have observed the power of peer-to-peer learning networks, where employees develop and share ideas for AI adoption. Take an article in Harvard Business Review about AI usage at the European bank BBVA: “Instead of relying on the core IT and operations functions, the organization empowered the people who understood business processes best to design the solutions.”

While leaders can create a framework for AI adoption, starting with clear business priorities, they also need to tap employees for their ideas and insights into where and how tools can truly improve internal processes and the customer experience. Whether it’s an online forum, a Slack conversation, or a weekly all-hands meeting, make sure there’s a channel where employees can contribute their perspectives on AI development and share best practices. 

Make trade-offs deliberately

Organization-wide change requires investments of both time and money. That’s why I recommend encouraging employees to build slack into their schedules to test and experiment with new tools and figure out how to streamline their workflows. Each step eliminated, each minute of busywork recaptured makes a difference—and the benefits compound over time.

Recognizing that every AI initiative competes for limited time, budget, and attention helps organizations decide where to invest more wisely. Experts recommend managing AI investments like a portfolio, evaluating each one against objective criteria. Consider whether an investment serves broader business goals, whether additional training is needed, what other resources are required, and the cost of diverting those resources. As they assess potential investments, leaders can also track whether their overall AI strategy is delivering returns. As noted in another HBR article, “The goal is to ensure that individual projects advance business strategy and that the overall mix of investments creates sustainable value.”

Ultimately, this means being as deliberate about what to deprioritize as what to pursue. Success with AI depends less on which tools companies adopt and more on their willingness to stay focused on the initiatives that matter most. Be lazy about how much you take on, and smart about what you choose.

#10412. How to clock out psychologically—and leave the bad vibes at work

It’s hard to leave work stress where it belongs: at work. 

Stressful days spent navigating tense conversations with coworkers or clients, or staring down an endless to-do list or email queue, can cause rumination, anxiety, and even after-hours work. Your job anxiety can easily, and frequently, spill into your personal life.

To break the cycle, experts suggest creating a wind-down routine.

Understanding Emotional Residue and Rumination

Our brains are hardwired to replay unfinished business, which is why you can’t just turn off your thoughts after a tough day at work. Forcing yourself to stop thinking about a stressful situation usually backfires, and this can exacerbate your worry. 

“Trying not to think about it, generally does not work, as our brains will latch harder onto anything we’re trying to push out,” notes psychologist Meera Khan, clinical director at the mental health treatment company LifeStance Health in Bensalem, Pennsylvania.

Without a solid routine to wrap up your workday, spillover stress easily creeps into dinner time and ruins the rest of your night, according to the Journal of Occupational Health Psychology.

“When something upsetting happens at work, the stress doesn’t automatically disappear just because the workday is over,” explains neuropsychologist Sanam Hafeez, director of the neuropsychological assessment practice Comprehend the Mind in New York. “Your mind will oftentimes replay the moment over and over, trying to make sense of what happened,” she says. 

To break free from that mental loop, research published in the journal Acta Psychologica highlights a few simple strategies: First, acknowledge how you are feeling. Then, write it down or talk it through with someone. Finally, give yourself permission to step away and leave whatever is unfinished for tomorrow.

Simple Routines to Help You Unwind After Work

Having a noticeable routine at the end of the day signals your brain that work is over. Heading home used to give us a natural break, but working from home doesn’t give the same type of break. 

“Commuting is stressful, and it often means packed buses and standing in traffic,” points out Manuela Collis, assistant professor of organization and strategy at Carnegie Mellon University’s Heinz College in Pittsburgh. “But the commute also did something useful for us: It created a temporal and physical boundary between what happens at work and life outside of it,” she says.

If there’s no commute, create new ways to wind down on your next WFH day. Stroll outside for a few minutes, walk your dog, or listen to an audiobook or podcast.

And then, after you log off, instead of dwelling on work issues all night, set a firm cutoff point and shift your focus to your personal life. “I recommend taking a few minutes at the end of each workday to write down anything that’s bothering you—that way, you have a clear plan for what to tackle the next day,” suggests Hafeez, who has a PsyD degree in school-community psychology.

Another tactic is to create a buffer. Before signing off, take two minutes to write down any worrisome tasks or stressors so they don’t linger in your head all night; putting something on paper can help transition it out of your mind, at least for now. Here are a few other simple ways to bridge the gap between work and your personal time.

  • Change your outfit: Take off your work clothes and put on comfy clothing. 
  • Take a 10-minute walk: Unplug, step away from your screen, and get some fresh air. 
  • Don’t feel compelled to check email: This one can be hard, given our 24/7 availability and smartphone culture—but the messages will be there tomorrow. So step away for tonight. 

The science backs this up. Per a study published in Frontiers in Psychology, participants who use such “sensory transition rituals” reduce work-life conflict by nearly half compared with those who are constantly on their devices. 

And if work stress still manages to sneak back in, it could be helpful to give yourself a finite time to worry.

“If you find yourself replaying work stress after hours, ask yourself if the issue is something you can solve right now,” advises Khan, who has a PsyD degree in clinical psychology. “I recommend a simple five-to-10-minute rule: If you can address it in five to 10 minutes, go ahead and do it. If not, let it wait,” she says.

Setting Boundaries and Normalizing Recovery Culture

As you make the shifts necessary to preserve your health and mental wellness, don’t feel guilty about it. This is time to reclaim your evenings and set boundaries. And when you work remotely, these blurred lines can make it a wee more challenging—especially given our culture of workaholism—but not impossible. 

“Working from home can make it feel like you’re expected to be available all the time,” Hafeez says. “But being a good employee doesn’t mean you have to be available 24/7.” Physical boundaries matter just as much as mental ones. “If you have the space or privilege to set up a dedicated workspace, try to keep all work-related activities contained to that area,” Khan suggests.

Leadership plays a key role, too. Managers need to practice what they preach and show their teams that staying online around the clock isn’t a badge of honor. 

“To help teams truly disconnect, managers can avoid scheduling late-day meetings, queue emails to send during regular working hours, and be crystal clear about expectations—especially what isn’t expected,” Collis notes.

The Bottom Line

The bad vibes shouldn’t follow you home; it’s okay to want to have calm evenings. Everyone is telling us to be more mindful and to preserve our headspace, but it isn’t an easy proposition. Clocking out from your work isn’t just about closing your laptop; it’s about creating meaningful and impactful ways to disconnect from work and keep tomorrow out of tonight.

Less than a week after Jensen Huang resigned from the company, Nvidia's board has created its own National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee. According to its announcement, the new standing committee will provide high-level oversight of Nvidia’s “national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risk management,” with its National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team reporting directly to the group and to interim CEO Colette Kress.

“Nvidia recognizes that advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and superintelligence present unprecedented challenges for national security,” Nvidia chairperson Harvey Jones said. “As the world’s leading advanced computing company, Nvidia has both a responsibility and an opportunity to lead the industry in addressing these challenges. We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation.”

The rumors of Jensen Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy, have thrown the company into turmoil, especially after his admission and subsequent apology. People have begun digging into details about Ms. Huang, revealing that she was at the center of a tangled web of companies and was reportedly instrumental in importing around $7.5 billion of banned Nvidia chips into China. A deeper investigation also revealed that her husband, Kang Wei, was behind her rise to prominence and seemingly accepted her relationship with the billionaire. It remains unclear if the couple made these shrewd business moves purely for profit or if they were under the control of a hidden third party, but it has certainly exposed the company to additional scrutiny.

The chairpersons of the House committees on China, Foreign Affairs, and Intelligence have since invited Jensen to a closed-door briefing to discuss Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage,” while President Donald Trump mentioned that the FBI is looking into Jensen Huang’s relationship with Ms. Huang. The U.S. first applied export controls to Nvidia’s most advanced chips, the A100 and H100, in 2022, forcing the company to create the China-market A800 and H800 GPUs that complied with Washington’s performance limitations.

However, the White House lowered the bar once more in 2023, which resulted in the even more watered-down H20, which, nonetheless, remained in high demand. Even though the Trump administration did not implement Biden’s AI diffusion rule, which threatened to outright ban several countries from buying Nvidia AI chips, the president eventually banned the export of H20 chips to China from April to June 2025.

Even before Trump’s total Nvidia AI GPU ban, there have already been multiple reports of smuggling, with one semiconductor analysis firm tracking more than 1.5 gigawatts of banned AI chips exported to China and estimating that up to 1.5 million Nvidia GPUs were smuggled in recent years. Despite that, the former Nvidia chief has always denied the allegations, saying that “There’s no evidence of any AI chip diversion.” Whether the allegations are true or not, it seems that the company is taking the situation seriously and taking steps to plug any leaks. As for Jensen Huang, he may be out of the company, but he still has to face Congress and all ongoing investigations.

#10409. Apple is turning your iPhone into a car key for 3 popular brands. Unlocking is only the beginning

Cadillac, Chevrolet, and GMC drivers will now be able to unlock their vehicles with their phones.

As first reported by MacRumors, General Motors announced that it has begun rolling out the Apple Wallet feature to select models. More vehicles are expected to be added over time. Eligible customers will receive notifications in the “What’s New” section of their vehicle’s app when digital-key support is available. 

Users will be able to use their smartphones or Apple Watches much like a physical key to unlock their vehicles. GM said supported vehicles will automatically unlock as a driver approaches and lock as the driver walks away. According to the company, the vehicle’s trunk and climate control system will be accessible with the new Apple Wallet feature. 

“The digital key experience will continue to evolve beyond simply unlocking and starting a vehicle. By leveraging ultra-wideband technology, GM is laying the groundwork for more deeply integrated and personalized experiences like automatically adjusting vehicle settings as drivers approach and other intelligent features that make ownership more convenient,” said the company in a press release.

Apple first announced the concept at its Worldwide Developers Conference in June 2020. It later launched exclusively for select 2021 BMW 5 Series models. Since then, the tech company has added other major automakers, such as Mercedes-Benz, Hyundai, Kia, Genesis, and Audi, to the offering.

The digital key may work even when a phone’s battery is dead. The company said that depending on a user’s iPhone model, keys could still be available even when a device needs to be charged. However, it warned that they will be available only for up to five hours.

The evolution of digital keys

Samsung rolled out its own version of the digital keys in 2021. In October, Samsung announced it would support digital keys for select GM vehicles. 

The digital key is the latest evolution in car-key technology. In the 1980s, automakers began using radio frequencies to create remote keyless entry fobs. 

In 2008, Nissan and tech company Sharp launched a mobile phone with a built-in intelligent car-key chip in Japan. Then, in 2017, Tesla advanced the concept by making its smartphone app the primary, default key for the Model 3, replacing the standard physical key fob. 

Apple and GM did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

#10408. How to Use Developer Time Tracking Data to Improve Sprint Planning and Estimates

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sprint estimates usually fail because development teams heavily rely on memory and assumptions instead of evidence. They assume similar tasks will take the same amount of time. Based on these half-baked assumptions, most managers plan around ideal sprint working hours. The backlog then fills with commitments that look realistic on paper but often end up delayed.

Actual development rarely follows that plan. There are always unexpected bugs and task dependencies that consume more time than teams account for in their estimates. Even the buffer time set aside for unexpected work may not be enough. This causes tasks to take longer than expected and pushes sprint commitments behind schedule.

Developer time tracking helps teams make better estimates with historical data. It shows how long previous tasks actually took, which provides managers with an evidence-based reference when they are planning similar work.

Reviewing this data before committing to a sprint scope turns estimation from guesswork into an evidence-based process.

Historical time data offers deeper insights, depending on how you collect and analyze it. Most importantly, it explains why planned work took longer than expected.

Before sprint planning, the following records should be reviewed.

Completed task duration: Check the time spent on finished tasks. Managers should compare similar work to understand typical development effort.

Actual versus estimated hours: Management should observe and identify differences between planned and recorded hours. If there are repeated delays, to some extent, it indicates inaccurate estimates.

Carryover work: Review unfinished tasks from previous sprints. Determine whether poor estimates or external delays caused the spillover..

Interruptions: Measure time spent on urgent requests and production issues. These activities reduce the development capacity that you had planned earlier.

Meetings and ceremonies: Review the time being spent on planning sessions and sprint reviews.

Bug-fix time: Examine hours spent resolving defects. You can also compare it to the time for developing new features.

Blocked tasks: Managers should account for the tasks delayed by missing approvals or technical dependencies.

Capacity differences: Compare team availability across sprints. Include leave and staffing changes in that time as well.

These records provide the most value when reviewed together. For example, a task may finish three days late even if the development work stayed within its estimated hours. The actual issue could be an external dependency.

Teams should understand these differences before using historical data to estimate future work.

Historical records provide a useful starting point for estimating new tasks. However, teams must interpret the data rather than simply copy previous estimates.

The following approaches can improve estimation accuracy.

The first step is to consider completed tasks that resemble upcoming work. Managers should compare their requirements and technical complexity. Moreover, the development environment should be considered.

For example, suppose a team needs to estimate a new API integration. Three previous integrations required 12, 15, and 18 hours of active work.

The average is 15 hours. This gives developers a reference point for the new estimate.

However, the average doesn't tell the entire story. The new integration may involve unfamiliar authentication methods or more complicated testing.

Review the reasons behind differences in previous task durations. Check whether developers encountered unexpected bugs or unclear requirements.

As a project manager, I'd consider these details before estimating for the next project. In my experience, they provide more context than an average alone.

Inaccurate estimates can happen; it doesn’t mean that there is a definite planning problem. However, repeated overruns across similar tasks may reveal an underlying issue.

Research suggests the pattern is widespread. A review of software estimation surveys reports that 60–80% of software projects encounter effort overruns, with the average overrun falling between 30% and 40%.

Start by calculating the difference between estimated and actual effort. Here is the formula for it.

Estimation variance (%) = [(Actual hours − Estimated hours) ÷ Estimated hours] × 100

Suppose a task was estimated at 10 hours but needed 14 hours. The actual effort exceeded the estimate by 40%.

You can compare the results across similar tasks.

For example, database migrations may repeatedly require more time than expected. This means that the team might be overlooking data validation or additional testing. Once the cause is clear, adjust future estimates accordingly.

Avoid increasing every estimate by the same percentage. Different types of work involve different risks. Teams can also break large tasks into smaller parts. This makes hidden development activities easier to identify.

The aim is to correct recurring estimation errors without unnecessarily increasing the entire sprint backlog.

Task duration doesn't always reflect the hours spent developing a feature.

A study of developer workdays by Meyer and colleagues, which tracked 2,197 hours of activity across 20 developers, found that coding accounted for around 21% of the typical day. Collaborative work such as meetings and email took up roughly 24%.

Consider a developer who starts a feature on Monday and finishes it on Wednesday. The task took three days to complete. This is pretty straightforward, and the estimation could be based on it; however, the developer may have spent several hours in meetings. Other than that, urgent support requests could also have consumed additional time.

The actual development effort could be much lower than three full working days. This distinction matters during estimation.

Teams should record focused development time separately from interruptions. They should also track waiting periods caused by blocked tasks. A more appropriate approach would be to use active development hours to estimate similar future work. They should also account for recurring interruptions when calculating sprint capacity.

For example, a task may regularly wait for security approval. Adding more development hours to its estimate won't resolve that delay.

Instead, the team should recognize the dependency and consider its effect on delivery.

If managers are able to separate these activities, it will help create better estimates without confusing effort with elapsed time.

A precise estimate can create false confidence when a task involves substantial uncertainty.

Suppose similar tasks previously required between 12 and 20 hours. If you estimate the next task at exactly 14 hours, it will overlook important differences.

A range of 12–20 hours provides a clearer picture of the possible effort. Developers can then discuss what might push the task toward either end of the range.

For example, the lower estimate can be directly applied to integration, and the upper estimate might be considered for unfamiliar code or additional testing.

In such scenarios, if the requirements stay unclear, consider a short technical investigation before finalizing the estimate. This can help identify dependencies and reduce uncertainty.

However, estimate ranges should still support practical planning decisions. Teams need to determine how much capacity to reserve for the work.

Choose a planning assumption that reflects the task's risk and available capacity.

As developers learn more about the task, they can refine the estimate.

Historical time data should affect how much work a team accepts during sprint planning. Better estimates offer little value if teams continue making unrealistic commitments.

If several sprints end with unfinished tasks, it is best that you first review why the team missed its commitments in the first place. Once you have identified the causes, use those findings to reduce the next sprint's scope.

Teams should prioritize work that supports the sprint goal. Moreover, avoid adding extra tasks just because they appear manageable during planning.

Production incidents and urgent requests can disrupt planned development. To get more reliable estimations, review how much time these activities consumed in previous sprints. Then reserve an appropriate amount of capacity.

Historical estimates become less reliable in case unfamiliar technology or additional dependencies are involved. It is best to break complex tasks into smaller components where possible. This helps developers assess the work more accurately.

Nominal capacity represents scheduled working hours, whereas actual capacity reflects the time available after accounting for other commitments.

The Scrum Guide identifies previous performance and upcoming capacity as important inputs to sprint forecasting.

When you are selecting backlog items, consider both. Additionally, avoid committing every available hour or deducting the same interruption twice.

Historical time data is useful for sprint planning. Most development teams already use project management tools that include basic time tracking features.

However, these tools don't always break down how developers spend their working hours. For clearer time data, a feature-specific time tracker is more useful because it provides more details about tasks and workloads.

TimeBee is one such developer time tracking tool I've used. It tracks working hours and time spent on projects and tasks. It also provides attendance records and workforce activity reports.

With this data, teams can review how much time previous tasks required. For example, developers can record hours spent building a feature. They can also track debugging and revisions separately. Later, managers can compare these records with the original estimates. This helps them plan similar work more accurately.

TimeBee also tracks website and application activity. These reports can help teams understand how working hours are distributed.

However, not all activities reflect actual development effort. Sometimes a developer just spends time reviewing documentation or discussing technical problems. Such work may not always appear in TimeBee as active computer use.

Apart from that, attendance, leave, and overtime records from TimeBee can help managers calculate sprint capacity. They can review developer availability before deciding how much work to include in the next sprint.

One thing to remember is that developer time tracking should help teams understand workload patterns. It shouldn't be used to monitor every minute of a developer's day. Management should be careful that the aim is to improve estimates and make more realistic sprint commitments.

Sprint retrospectives should include a review of how the planning is going. If you have made a plan, it doesn’t mean you cannot make changes to it. During sprints, keep comparing original estimates with actual task hours. Track your unfinished work for recurring delays.

Ask developers what caused significant differences. Some tasks may have required additional testing. Others may have been delayed by dependencies. Select one specific improvement for the next sprint.

Not every estimation difference indicates a planning failure. Unexpected technical challenges are part of software development.

The objective is to improve forecasts over time rather than eliminate every variance.

Historical time data provides a more stable foundation for sprint planning. Developer time tracking helps teams understand what is actually happening within the sprint rather than creating unnecessary pressure for them.

Other than that, the data also reveals how interruptions affect available development hours.

However, time data should guide planning rather than dictate it.

1. What is the difference between sprint velocity and time-based capacity planning?

Sprint velocity measures how much work a team has completed during a sprint. It is usually measured in story points. Contrary to this, time-based capacity planning calculates the hours available for planned work. It accounts for meetings and other responsibilities.

Velocity helps predict future delivery based on past performance. Capacity planning shows whether the team has enough time to meet its commitments.

2. Which time tracking metrics are most useful for improving Agile sprint forecasts? The most useful metrics include estimated versus actual hours, task completion time, and unplanned work.

Bug-fix time, rework, and blocked tasks also provide valuable insights. Teams should also review available capacity across previous sprints.

These metrics help sort out recurring delays and estimation errors. They allow teams to forecast workloads more accurately and make realistic sprint commitments.

**3. How can development teams improve estimates when historical time tracking data is incomplete? **

Teams can start with available task records and completed sprint backlogs. Developer feedback can help fill information gaps. Similar tasks from previous projects may also provide useful estimates.

When data is limited, teams should use estimate ranges instead of fixed hours. Consistent time tracking in future sprints will gradually provide more reliable planning data.

4. How can time tracking data help balance workloads across developers during sprint planning?

Time tracking data shows how much time developers spend on assigned tasks and other responsibilities. Managers can review these records to identify uneven workloads. They can then distribute upcoming tasks based on available capacity.

Technical expertise and task complexity should also influence assignments. This helps prevent over commitment and supports a more balanced workload across the development team.

#10407. Google Maps rolling out travel itineraries & list search for Ask Maps

Ahead of the holiday season, Google Maps is launching a handy travel itineraries feature alongside a slew of other new capabilities for Ask Maps.

Ask Maps can now build travel itineraries that feature numbered map pins for each stop. It supports everything from shopping excursions to multi-day road trips with several stops. When used for the latter, Google Maps will generate a day-by-day schedule with tips and the numbered pins that aid visualization. Plans can be shared with others and exported to Google Docs on desktop.

Once on the trip, Ask Maps will show directions and real-time details, including live traffic conditions, whether a place is open, and “even what the vibe is at your next stop.” You can conversationally have Google add more stops to the itinerary.

Meanwhile, Ask Maps can now tap into your saved lists to find bookmarked places and take action. This lets you ask: “Which spots saved in my lists have availability for five people in the next 30 minutes?”

Before you start directions, you’ll see familiar “Know Before You Go” tips that surface information about your route, like parking locations, car charging options, weather, potential delays, and tolls.

New agentic capabilities let Ask Maps find online beauty, pet care, auto, and home repair appointments, as well as call local businesses on your behalf. For example, “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me” returns a list of open slots.

Finally, Ask Maps is expanding to 30 more countries across Europe, including Spain, Germany, and the UK.

These updates are rolling out starting today on Google Maps for Android and iOS. Travel itineraries and list search are available in all 200+ Ask Maps countries. Know Before You Go in directions and appointment booking are coming first to the US.

#10406. Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron form unlikely alliance to standardize robot charging as chipmakers push toward unmanned fabs

Semiconductor manufacturers are increasing automation to boost the productivity of existing fabs

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Samsung Electronics, SK hynix, and Micron are reportedly working together to develop common charging standards for mobile robots used in semiconductor fabrication plants, according to a new report. Representatives from the three companies have reportedly formed an early-stage consultative body to lead standardization efforts, alongside major industry stakeholders such as the Semiconductor Equipment and Materials International (SEMI) industry association.

According to a report by Seoul Economic Daily, the initiative aims to establish common technical specifications that would allow robots from different manufacturers to share charging equipment, reducing the cost and complexity of deploying large robotic fleets across semiconductor manufacturing facilities. The broader goal is to accelerate factory automation, particularly in older fabs, while laying the groundwork for fully autonomous semiconductor manufacturing.

So why are three of the world's biggest memory manufacturers, who are also competitors, coming together to establish standards for the robotics industry? What exactly does the collaboration involve? And what are the implications of something as seemingly minor as robot charging for the broader semiconductor and robotics industries?

Soaring demand for semiconductor memory chips used in AI infrastructure has driven manufacturers to automate as many production processes as possible to optimize manufacturing speed and capacity in existing facilities to increase output, while they build additional fabs. Modern semiconductor fabs already have extensive automation systems. However, even these facilities still require human workers for certain operations, such as moving materials between floors and unpacking products, that existing automation systems cannot perform. The issue is even more pronounced in older fabs, which generally have fewer automated material-handling systems and still rely on workers to move wafer containers using manual carts.

One potential solution is to hand these remaining manual operations over to mobile robots, allowing manufacturers to automate tasks without undertaking extensive renovations or installing complex fixed transport systems. These could include autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) that transport materials around the factory, mobile manipulators that combine robotic arms with moving platforms, and humanoid robots capable of performing more complicated handling tasks.

The problem, however, is that these robots come in different builds and configurations, often with their own batteries and accompanying charging infrastructure. A semiconductor fab deploying multiple robot models from different manufacturers could consequently end up requiring separate charging stations for each model. In addition to increasing equipment and maintenance costs, these installations consume valuable factory floor space.

The proposed initiative seeks to address this problem by establishing common charging specifications that different robot manufacturers can adopt. Standardized charging infrastructure would allow multiple types of robots to use compatible charging stations, reducing the need for separate installations and making it easier for semiconductor manufacturers to expand their robotic fleets without adding operational inefficiencies.

The alliance is considering standards covering battery specifications for different mobile robots, charging-station equipment and communication protocols, charging connectors, and battery management systems (BMS). Together, these specifications would establish common requirements for the physical and electronic interfaces involved in charging robots inside semiconductor fabs.

The initial objective is to achieve charging compatibility across different robot models. In addition to letting a fab deploy robots from several manufacturers without having to install a separate charging system for every model, this would also give manufacturers greater flexibility when purchasing new robots, since their choice of supplier would no longer be as heavily influenced by the charging infrastructure already installed in the facility.

A subsequent step would involve integrating robot charging data with the fab's manufacturing execution system (MES), the software that coordinates and monitors manufacturing operations. With access to information such as battery charge levels, robot availability, and production schedules, the system could coordinate when individual robots operate and when they return for charging. For example, robots could be scheduled to recharge during periods of lower demand or while other robots handle critical material transfers, minimizing interruptions to production. This integration would become increasingly important as manufacturers deploy larger fleets of robots across the hundreds of individual processes involved in semiconductor fabrication.

Interestingly, the three chipmakers leading the standardization efforts are primarily customers of industrial robotics manufacturers, not manufacturers of the robots themselves, except for Samsung, which has an established robotics business. The objective is to develop specifications that robotics manufacturers and charging-equipment suppliers can incorporate into their products.

On the other hand, the three companies are not independently creating specifications and dictating them to suppliers. The initiative would likely follow an industry standardization process in which robotics manufacturers, equipment suppliers, and other stakeholders contribute to developing and validating the technical requirements. For now, the project remains in its early stages, with participants still determining which components and interfaces should be standardized and consulting robotics and smart-factory specialists.

According to DigiTimes, semiconductor industry participants first explored establishing common robotics standards roughly a decade ago, but discussions made little progress until recently. The renewed momentum is largely attributed to the ongoing semiconductor boom, which has coincided with rapid advancements in industrial robotics.

Unprecedented demand for AI-related memory products, along with record financial performance, has given semiconductor manufacturers both the incentive and the financial resources to invest more aggressively in factory automation. While manufacturers are expanding production capacity to meet demand, new fabs take years to construct and bring online. As a result, they are simultaneously looking to squeeze out as much capacity as possible from existing facilities by increasing automation and improving productivity.

As for why Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron are collaborating despite their intense rivalry, the answer likely comes down to shared commercial interests. Incompatible robot charging infrastructure is an industry-wide problem, and all three companies stand to benefit from a common solution. The AI boom has already encouraged numerous partnerships across the semiconductor supply chain, including between companies that are considered fierce rivals, as manufacturers look for ways to overcome common production and infrastructure constraints.

The involvement of these particular companies also gives the initiative considerable weight. Together, Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron control almost the entire global DRAM market. They also operate extensive semiconductor manufacturing networks and represent a substantial potential market for fab-specific robotic equipment. A common set of specifications backed by all three would therefore provide robotics manufacturers with a strong commercial incentive to develop compatible products, potentially shortening development cycles and accelerating adoption.

Although the current collaboration focuses on a relatively small aspect of factory automation, it is a significant step for broader standardization across the semiconductor manufacturing and industrial robotics industries. Common charging infrastructure would make it easier to deploy and manage mixed robotic fleets, while future integration with production management systems could bring fabs closer to operating with minimal human intervention. This longer-term ambition of completely autonomous facilities is already taking shape. Both SK hynix and Samsung have outlined plans to develop an autonomous semiconductor fab by 2030.

#10405. The smartest AI might be the one that leaves us alone

One of the ideas I’m always trying to tell my students is that their brains are something, an asset, if you like, they need to protect. The human brain is an amazing optimizer: Provide it with an effortless way to achieve something, and it will quickly start to use it. We used to memorize a ton of phone numbers a few decades ago. Now we can hardly memorize our own, simply because our brain knows the number is a few clicks away. 

A clear example is why I never use AI to write my articles: simply because, for me, in my personal methodology as a professor of innovation, writing is my way of making concepts stick in my brain, concepts I will need later to teach and discuss. If I ask ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or any other chatbot to write my articles for me, I would lose much of the learning that writing gives me.

This doesn’t mean I don’t use AI: I can use it to translate certain parts, to search for relevant articles to back up an assertion, or to assess whether the concepts I try to explain come across clearly. But I don’t want to use it for writing, because writing is a skill I want to protect. And like a muscle, if you don’t exercise it, it quickly atrophies.

For a manager, the skill worth protecting might be decision-making: An AI that makes every choice could undermine precisely the judgment that person needs to develop. The useful behavior depends on the objective, and sometimes that objective requires the system to hold back. 

What happens when we move from personal to corporate use? Can an AI learn when its intervention would make things worse? That capability might receive very little applause in a product demonstration, but it could be enormously valuable in practice.

The sales agent that lets us be 

Imagine a company using a sales agent. When it identifies a customer approaching renewal, it follows a standard procedure: It quickly reviews the account, writes a personalized email, offers a discount, and schedules a follow-up. All of it in mere seconds. And the audience claps enthusiastically. 

But what if our customer would have renewed anyway? Then, the end result is that we have wasted an interaction, risked alienating the customer, and surrendered margin unnecessarily. What if our customer is a happy one, and the right thing to do would have been just to wait for him or her to renew voluntarily? 

Even when all tasks are perfectly executed, the decision to perform them could have been perfectly wrong. 

The cost of being helpful

We know how this feels when we’re working with real people: Experienced employees often develop a sense of when to follow up, when to escalate an issue, and when making too many interventions will look messy, send the wrong signal, or make the customer upset. How do they know that? It comes with experience; it’s learning that compounds over time, with more and more iterations.

That judgment is something we pay to have. However, when we evaluate AI, we tend to be fascinated with visible activity—with messages generated, tasks completed, workflows executed, etc. The equivalent is if we were dealing with a hyperactive employee. And as we probably know, someone who sends twice the number of messages is probably not twice as valuable. 

In other words, just because an action can be automated and, therefore, performed easily, doesn’t mean that we should be performing it all the time. 

Look what happens with AI coding assistants: In “When to show a suggestion? Integrating human feedback in AI-assisted programming,” Microsoft researchers used data from 535 programmers to retrospectively evaluate a system that selectively withheld suggestions that were apparently likely to be rejected by the developers. They also found that optimizing for suggestion acceptance could produce lower-quality suggestions. Getting people to accept more assistance was an imperfect measure of helping them. 

Learning when to intervene

In the case of our renewal agent, a system that learns from a lot of comparable cases could perhaps investigate which interventions help with whom. For instance, some customers don’t like the feeling of being “directed” or “influenced,” and are better left to their own devices. Some like a particular type of interaction through a particular channel, but they hate others. Or they want to talk to the same customer representatives every time because they remember them. 

The function to protect would be the ability to spot these cases. Do not automate; optimize. But optimization is not necessarily something that today’s corporate AI does well. Today’s corporate AIs can generate splendid emails, but following the before and after and deciding to do nothing is usually not an alternative. 

It’s the experience from all previous cases, processed along with the specific characteristics of every customer, that leads to the lessons learned, to the continuous improvement, to the process being optimized. And that ability to improve decisions through accumulated experience is precisely what you need. 

Give waiting a fair chance

When buying or deploying AI, managers should, therefore, find out what outcome the system is theoretically trying to improve, and design ways to know whether its actions helped or not. We need to be honest here: A renewal following an email does not necessarily establish that the email was the reason for the renewal. Customers differ, circumstances change, and useful comparisons may require carefully designed experiments. Simply storing more interaction histories will not settle the question. 

This includes maintaining the necessary human oversight, the now-famous “human-in-the-loop”: A missed warning or an unanswered complaint can be costly. People must define the obligations and limits within which the system can learn. 

I haven’t seen an AI system that reviews an account, checks all the available evidence from the corporate ERP or CRM, and decides that contacting the customer would probably make things worse. So the final outcome would be that nothing gets sent, no discount is offered, and we just let the customer evolve naturally. No hyperactivity. Why? Because our corporate learning optimized it, and the accumulated learning behind that decision should remain under our company’s control, available even if we replace the model or the vendor powering our agents.

It might be a disappointing demo. But it could be excellent business.
