#10403. Jeff Bezos’s $41 billion AI startup Prometheus is shrouded in secrecy. We found out who’s building it

For many in the tech industry, physical AI is the next world to conquer. While developers of large language models like OpenAI and Anthropic seek to push reasoning models distilled on billions of streams of text to their limits, an emerging crop of companies are focusing on an even more ambitious goal: developing AI programs designed to speak the language of physics. Should they succeed, these firms have a stake in everything from building models that might power self-driving manufacturing or enable drug discovery to those that can take on plane design and weapons development. 

The promise is enormous. Whoever cracks physical AI could control a slice of the software stack that becomes critical to a host of industries—and worth many, many billions. Already, a growing list of companies are racing to stake their claim. Among the buzziest is Prometheus, a startup backed by Jeff Bezos that’s already flush with cash.

Bezos isn’t just bankrolling Prometheus. He’s also coleading the company, marking his first executive role since stepping down as Amazon’s CEO in 2021. His cofounder is Vik Bajaj, a Stanford professor who previously led science operations at Verily, Alphabet’s health technology venture. Prometheus was incubated in 2024 at Foresite Labs, which Bajaj leads, with support from the venture capital firm Arch Venture Partners. A number of Prometheus employees also appear to have come from firms associated with Bajaj.

By combing through LinkedIn and researchers’ personal websites, Fast Company identified 130 people who say they’re currently working for Prometheus, and assembled what appears to be the first public database of its kind. Prometheus employs approximately 250 people, including numerous accomplished AI researchers, some of whose names have not been publicly disclosed. The company is recruiting not only AI model developers but also experts in fields like aerospace and chemistry, a strong hint that it may one day target manufacturing and healthcare customers. Employees bring expertise in ocean engineering, energy engineering, mathematics, and even high-performance computing.

In this Subscriber Exclusive, you’ll discover:

  • An exclusive database of the more than 130 people who have publicly joined Prometheus, Bezos’s buzzy and secretive AI startup
  • What those employees’ expertise tells us about where the company is headed, and direct insights from people within Prometheus about what they’re actually building
  • A list of rival companies competing in the physical AI space—and their investors
  • Deep insight into what physical AI actually is, and why the market could be worth hundreds of billions
  • Why Bezos’s other, more renowned companies, Amazon and Blue Origin, stand to benefit most if Prometheus succeeds

At a Semafor event on November 17, Bezos and Bajaj said they’ve spent much of their funding on compute and have built one single multi-physics model. Thus far, Prometheus has built a neural surrogate for numerical simulation and has used the technology to design a range of hardware, including an experiment that involved having the company’s models redesign the Mars helicopter.

This next AI revolution needs AI tools trained not on text but on data from the physical world, as well as subject-matter experts who can ensure that models are distilling a common core of engineering principles that can extend across myriad domains. This, in turn, involves recruiting not just AI coders but plenty of people with expertise in the physical realm, whether that’s manufacturing automotive parts or running biology labs.

“Most fundamentally, the biggest challenge is just the sheer breadth of what we’re doing. Engineering is vast. There’s no such thing as an engineer,” one leading AI expert and early-stage Prometheus employee, speaking on the condition of anonymity, tells Fast Company. “This idea of building something that’s general enough to cover all of that space, that’s been a really, really huge challenge—and a really interesting one.”

What Prometheus, and physical AI, aim to achieve

News that Prometheus (formerly called the Prometheus Project) was under development went public only last year, and its leadership has been tight-lipped about what it’s actually trying to build. We do know that the company was incubated at Foresite Labs, which is housed within the health and life sciences investment firm Foresite Capital. (In addition to Prometheus, Foresite Labs has backed companies like AI drug discovery startup Xaira and disease therapy outfit Alumis.)

Still, Prometheus’s bare-bones website includes only links to its LinkedIn and X pages, and government documents show that Prometheus used a code name (“FL2024-008 INC”) for a small amount of lobbying and when applying for H1-B visas for some employees.

We also know that Prometheus has attracted significant capital from investors interested in healthcare, AI, and tech manufacturing. The company originally raised about $6 billion in funding, and then another $12 billion—for a $41 billion valuation—earlier this year. Its backers, Semafor reported in June, include JPMorgan; BlackRock; and Arch Venture Partners. Other backers include Powerlaw, a closed-end fund that has also invested in high-tech companies like SpaceX, Colossal, and Waymo, as well as RoboStrategy, a venture capital fund that says it owns shares in the company.

Bezos has said that the company isn’t focused on robotics, though that’s what many people first associate with the term physical AI. Instead, Prometheus aims to develop what it calls an artificial general engineer, which Bezos likens to a much more advanced version of computer-aided design, or CAD, powered by artificial intelligence.

“My through line for the last few years has been AI,” Bezos said in an interview with Squawk Box anchor Andrew Ross Sorkin earlier this year. “My time at Amazon is spent on AI. My time at Prometheus is spent on AI—Prometheus is really an AI company. And my time at Blue [Origin] is largely spent on AI. And [at] Prometheus . . . the tools that we’re building are going to help companies like Blue immensely.”

A trademark application makes clear that Prometheus’s aspirations extend far beyond healthcare, spanning much of the engineering and manufacturing pipeline. The document references physical simulations and digital twin technology, along with structural, thermal, fluid, acoustic, and electromagnetic analysis, and even “acoustic and vibration analysis, noise prediction, and acoustic design optimization.” The application also discusses 3D printing, semiconductor manufacturing, and developing factory layouts.

It’s not hard to see why this interdisciplinary approach might one day prove lucrative. Companies spend an extraordinary amount of time researching and developing new components and hardware, a process that can involve the arduous work of finding and vetting suppliers. There’s also the expensive, resource-intensive process of simulating and testing how new systems perform once they’re built and under different conditions. Another challenge: developing production lines capable of manufacturing that hardware at scale.

Consider the development of a jet engine, a process that can require thousands of workers and more than a decade of design, prototyping, testing, and manufacturing. Prometheus envisions AI tools that could dramatically compress that timeline, from, say, a decade to just a few years. The company sees similar opportunities across everything from household products to large-scale industrial systems. 

The aspiration for the physical AI industry is to automate as much of the process as possible and make real-world testing and evaluation far more efficient. The idea is that this could speed up hardware development across a wide range of industries. Indeed, Prometheus reportedly already has its eyes on a network of spin-offs in which it might one day own stakes.

“Today it takes days to weeks for engineers to set up one simulation for one design. There are a lot of repetitive, manual, low-added-value tasks that they have to go through while using this software,” explains Thomas von Tschammer, cofounder of Neural Concept, a physical AI startup and Prometheus competitor. “The opportunity with AI is first of all to automate and compress a lot of this low-added-value work from those engineers so that they can actually spend time engineering.”

Inside Prometheus

One early Prometheus employee, an expert in neural networks who was among the company’s first hires, was excited to “get back to basics” and pursue fundamental research. At the Bezos-backed firm, the employee says he’s working on building an “end-to-end” system at the intersection of physics and AI, developing “accurate, high-fidelity simulations” that could help engineers with initial designs.

The goal, the employee says, is to create an agentic artificial engineer that could one day drive “simulations and use them to make design decisions at the highest level.” Such an AI system would ideally be generalizable across engineering disciplines, much as current LLMs can be applied to a wide range of text-based tasks and types of content.

“If we can get a tool that across many different domains is able to simulate faster and more accurately, you can see how this generalizes to fields that wouldn’t otherwise have had contact very much at all,” the Prometheus employee says.

A good number of staffers come from other major AI companies, including xAI, and many have particular experience in AI-based materials science. Notably, a number hail from companies where Bajaj was formerly affiliated, including Google, Foresite Labs, and Foresite-backed Xaira.

Before leaving Foresite, Bajaj helped incubate a range of biotech firms and filed a patent for AI-based nucleic acid sequencing. Several employees have also come to Prometheus from General Agents, the applied AI research lab that Prometheus quietly acquired last year. The lab released “Ace,” a real-time computer autopilot, last year, and its former CEO, Sherjil Ozair, is now on Prometheus’s technical staff.

Other staffers have far more eclectic backgrounds. In its quest to build powerful simulations, Prometheus has hired at least one former employee of video game developer Epic Games, and a former AI researcher from Meta’s Reality Labs. The company has also recruited employees from Waymo and Red Bull Advanced Technologies, which helps translate Formula 1 innovations into applications for the automotive and aerospace industries.

Prometheus’s hires also suggest that it may eventually want to sell to the government. The company’s team includes a technical adviser who also serves as a chief scientist for the U.S. Army’s ground systems research. Another Prometheus adviser is Chase Johnson, who previously served in the Marine Corps’ innovation unit and worked as an attorney for defense tech company Anduril. Johnson, in his LinkedIn bio, suggests Prometheus could one day transform the “defense industrial base.”

Another employee who works at Prometheus government relations tells Fast Company that what brought them to the Bezos-backed firm was the desire to work on “cutting-edge” problems. In particular, they’re interested in how an AI engineering agent could aid industries with critical supply chains, including the automotive and semiconductor sectors.

“We are entirely focused on building models and products for the physical economy, and to accelerate the dream to build loop,” the employee says. “We are exclusively focused on design, engineering, and manufacturing, and I think that is an advantage. Focus is always an advantage, and we know that we are purpose-built for design, engineering, and manufacturing.” 

The quest for physical AI

Bezos may already have a ready-made customer for Prometheus: himself. His space company, Blue Origin, is developing reusable rockets to launch satellites and humans into orbit, with ambitions that extend to orbital data centers. (At that Semafor event, Bezos said Blue Origin was already using some Prometheus tech.) All of that requires extensive manufacturing and engineering work, which could benefit from the kind of AI-powered software Prometheus is developing. Bezos has acknowledged the potential connection, though it remains unclear whether—or how—Prometheus might ultimately integrate with his other businesses.

Then there’s Amazon, which does plenty of its own in-house manufacturing, maintains frontier AI and robotics research groups, and has invested heavily in warehouse robotics. Bezos has also invested in Physical Intelligence, a startup developing AI models for the physical world and robotics, though there doesnt’ appear to be any formal relationship between the two companies. Taken together, these interests raise the possibility that Bezos is positioning himself to build a new, far-reaching empire centered on physical AI.

In the meantime, a range of other startups are competing in the physical AI race. Anima Anandkumar and Benedikt Jenik were once approached about leading Prometheus before launching their own startup, Accelerated Understanding. (That offer, Reuters previously reported, came from Bajaj and would have included a major stake in the company and a million-dollar salary.) Their focus is on building models capable of making predictions in four dimensions, at any resolution. To do that, they say they need a team that isn’t constrained by traditional disciplinary silos or the limitations of conventional LLMs.

“Even if one were to use LLMs to automate execution, the real world stays the bottleneck,” Anandkumar tells Fast Company. “If we instead teach AI models to directly simulate and understand physics, that bottleneck goes away.”

Other firms envision a similar formula for building physical AI teams: a mix of machine learning generalists and specialists with engineering and manufacturing experience.

Paul Eremenko, of P-1 AI, which makes an agentic AI tool called Archie that works directly within engineering teams, argues that it’s often much easier to train someone with an aerospace background in the latest AI research than to teach an AI specialist the nuances of aerospace engineering.

“We don’t compete with OpenAI or Anthropic for talent,” Eremenko says. “The prototypical AI researcher or AI engineer for us is somebody who comes from a physical world background—a mechanical engineer, aerospace engineer, electrical engineer—who became very interested in AI.”

Back at Prometheus, the competition for talent is only expected to intensify. An employee working in government relations tells Fast Company that the Prometheus expects to expand its workforce exponentially, even as hiring remains highly selective. For the early employee specializing in AI, the recruiting pitch comes down to the opportunity to tackle problems that have long eluded conventional engineering tools. “In terms of wooing them, I think I’m often selling people on the novelty and the excitement.”

The Fugaku supercomputer, operated by the national research institute Riken, has been breached, with users' data, including names, emails, and more, stolen.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Fugaku, Japan's most powerful supercomputer and the ninth-fastest on the planet, has suffered a suspected data breach. The news was announced by its operator, Riken, which is the country's national research institute, with the outfit also confirming that personal information relating to more than 4,000 users of Fugaku was potentially taken during the breach. Further, the information of 375 users of Riken's Rikyu AI supercomputer was also possibly taken. The personal information includes names, email addresses, research files, and even the authentication information that was used to access the supercomputers and related services. The Japan Times reports that the operators of Fugaku first became aware of suspicious communications on November 12, with those suspicions then triggering an investigation.

By November 14, the investigation had confirmed that unauthorized access to Fugaku had taken place, with access also blocked at that time. The investigation identified that hackers had used the supercomputer's externally accessible operational status dashboard as the springboard for the hack between November 10 and November 13. Now taken offline while security concerns are addressed, the dashboard allowed the hackers to gain access to the system's internal network, but beyond that, details are scarce. Riken does not yet know — or at least, it isn't saying — the full story of how the hackers gained access to Fugaku as a whole. But it has confirmed that some servers had unauthorized software installed.

Following the discovery of the breach, Riken reported the incident to Japan's Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT). Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara has since confirmed that MEXT and Riken were working together to investigate what happened and ascertain the full scope of the breach itself. “Fugaku plays a vital role in our country’s research and development infrastructure, so it is important that they prioritize security while limiting the impact on research activities,” Kihara is reported to have said.

Located at Riken’s Center for Computational Science in Kobe, Fugaku officially came online in March of 2021 after being developed in collaboration with Fujitsu for a cost of around ¥130 billion (approximately $817 million in 2026). It became the world's fastest supercomputer before being overtaken by Frontier, an exascale supercomputer housed at the Department of Energy's Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility (OLCF) in Tennessee.

The fastest supercomputer currently in operation is China's LineShine. It recently retained its crown as the fastest on the planet amid a move away from traditional supercomputers to AI data centers.

#10400. Anthropic’s IPO asks investors to bet that a product can build a company, not the other way around

When Anthropic launches its initial public offering this Thursday, it will be another test of how much further the AI industry’s seemingly unchecked growth can go. The company is seeking a valuation of $1.4 trillion, asking investors to buy into the idea that artificial intelligence will become a major contributor to the economy.

But the IPO also asks investors to make a more unusual bet: on a company whose own product could eventually do much of the work of building the business itself.

In its amended S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, released last week, Anthropic says that “each new version of a Claude model directly accelerates development of the next.” Claude already helps run experiments, generate training data, and test future models, the company says. As evidence, Anthropic notes that Claude wrote more than 90% of contributions to its code base in September 2026. In the three-month period through September, the daily volume of code contributed per engineer was more than 45 times its 2024 average.

Traditionally, companies go public asking investors to bankroll employees who will build and sell better products. Anthropic is pitching something different: a business whose products increasingly help develop their own successors—and, in the process, help build the company itself.

There is some precedent for a company using its own technology to improve it. When the software company GitLab went public in 2021, its prospectus described how employees used GitLab’s development platform to identify problems and determine what to build next, a practice known as “dogfooding.” But that was software helping human developers do their jobs, rather than AI increasingly performing the work itself.

“It may be the first IPO in which this type of thing is happening,” says Sinan Aral, a professor at MIT Sloan School of Management.

Still, Aral cautions against confusing AI’s growing role in developing products with the ability to decide which products should exist in the first place. Claude may be writing code, but humans remain responsible for the more consequential research decisions. “What to do, what goals to have and what to optimize, is generally being decided by human beings,” he says.

Even so, experts say Anthropic’s pitch represents a striking departure from the conventional IPO. Until now, discussions of recursive self-improvement—the idea that AI systems could improve their own capabilities—have largely centered on the risks of systems becoming misaligned with human goals, says Jay Ritter, director of the IPO Initiative at the University of Florida’s Warrington College of Business.

But Ritter sees a potentially transformative business opportunity, too. Unlike conventional processes of innovation, which often yield diminishing returns, AI-driven self-improvement could theoretically produce exponential gains. That would fundamentally change not only how products are developed, but how the companies behind them operate.

“Anthropic and its competitors are companies that are increasingly capable of building themselves,” Ritter says. “Investors are essentially being asked to pay for the electricity to do this.”

The prospect also raises questions about how much autonomy Anthropic is willing to grant Claude—and whether a system capable of directing its own development would make decisions aligned with human interests. For now, MIT’s Aral says, the company appears reluctant to surrender that control. Its S-1 contains “a risk section like we’ve never read before,” he says, reflecting the possibility that its technology could eventually begin making consequential decisions on its own.

Not everyone is convinced that such a future is imminent, or even plausible. Kirill Skrygan, CEO of JetBrains, a company known for its software development tools, is skeptical that Anthropic has created an AI system capable of improving itself without human intervention. He also disputes the notion that Anthropic represents an entirely new kind of business, one whose development could eventually escape human control.

“I think it’s more about hype before the IPO,” he says.

Indeed, a closer reading of Anthropic’s filing reveals a more qualified vision than its headline figures might suggest. The company acknowledges that errors in existing models could carry over into future ones, and says it does not expect to let Claude develop successive frontier models without meaningful human supervision—at least not yet.

Whether Anthropic can deliver on its vision of AI increasingly building the business behind it remains an open question. Investors who buy the stock this week will be betting that it can, even as the company itself acknowledges the risks and limitations of that ambition.

#10398. The best kids’ gifts of 2026 are all about screen-free calm

Over the past decade, waking up on Christmas morning with kids involved a cacophony of beeping robots, singing plush toys, and gadgets flashing every color of the rainbow. (Until somebody quietly “lost” the batteries.)

For years, toy makers have packed their products with tech designed to keep kids engaged. Tablets autoplayed the next episode, and apps were engineered to keep kids hooked. But parents have had enough, especially after a growing pile of research has linked heavy screen use to all kinds of problems in children. Families are now hunting for ways to help their kids slow down and regulate their nervous systems.

But there’s a growing consensus among scientists and developmental psychologists that the problem isn’t technology itself; it’s that companies are engineering these devices to addict kids. And a new generation of toy designers is flipping the script. They’re incorporating technology to calm kids down, rather than rev them up, swapping out feeds and autoplays for calming music and stories. This new “quiet tech” movement has produced some of the most innovative products on the market.

For this year’s guide, I rounded up my favorite examples of gifts that soothe instead of overstimulate. Most are completely screen-free. I’ve arranged them to follow the arc of a kid’s day, from the first yawn to lights out. Your own nervous system may thank you, too.

Getting Out the Door Without a Meltdown
Skylight, Skylight Buddy, $139.99 (plus $39 per year for Buddy Plus after the first free month)

In many homes, mornings are incredibly stressful, as parents struggle to get kids to do the most basic tasks to get out the door on time. Skylight Buddy was created to solve this problem.

It’s a small bedside device featuring a friendly character that walks kids through their morning, after-school, and bedtime routines. Buddy is also an alarm clock, a night-light, and a white noise machine that shuts off on its own in the morning. Its OK-to-wake light changes color so a kid knows they can get out of the room and wake the rest of the family up. The optional Buddy Plus plan adds star rewards, a visual timer, and messages from parents that Buddy reads aloud. It’s designed for ages 4 to 10.

The Calm of Knowing What Happens Next
Charmspring, SpringboardGo Large, $95

Research shows that kids feel calmer when they know what’s coming next in their day. Charmspring’s SpringboardGo is a magnetic board that maps out a child’s day and week, with 194 magnetic tiles that show different tasks and activities, like “brush teeth” and “school.” Kids can help create the schedule, which helps them feel empowered. It’s a lighter, more compact version of the brand’s original Springboard, so it fits in smaller spaces. It also arrives in gift-ready packaging, which is one less thing to wrap.

Say Bonjour
Dex, Dex Language-Learning Camera, $249

Dex is a kids’ camera that doubles as a language tutor. Kids point it at everyday objects (an apple, a passing fire truck), and Dex will translate the word into the language they’re learning. If they snap a picture of the object, it adds more details like color, shape, and what the thing does. Dex covers 16 languages and more than 30 dialects, from Spanish and Mandarin to Hindi and Arabic, with levels from beginner to advanced. It has a small touchscreen, but the whole point is to get kids looking up at the world. It’s designed for ages 3 to 8.

No Opening Until Wheels Up
Parcel Air, Airplane Box, $68

Flying with kids can be a nightmare. Most parents resort to handing them a tablet and declaring unlimited screen time. But Parcel Air’s boxes are designed to create hours of screen-free entertainment for short and long-haul flights.

Each box holds four hand-numbered parcels wrapped in kraft paper and twine. Kids open them one at a time, and only once the plane is in the air. The boxes come in four age ranges, from 2 and under up to 8. The Navigator, for ages 6 to 8, includes a gear-building machine, an explorer’s book, group trivia, and a rocket to build on the descent. Younger kids get magnetic blocks, crafts, and finger puppets.

(Road-tripping instead? The Carpool box, from $38, is filled with toys that won’t scatter across the back seat.)

A beautiful spot to do activities
Piccalio, Arcc Kids Table & Chair Set, from $469

Calm kids need a quiet space in the home to come back to. Piccalio’s new Arcc set, designed by the celebrated furniture designer Hanne Willmann, aims to give little ones their own spot for drawing, puzzles, and snack time.

While many play tables are painted in primary colors and emblazoned in cartoon characters, this set takes its cues from 1970s Scandinavian modernism. It’s made of bent beech plywood with soft arches and rounded edges, and it comes in beech, walnut, tomato, or powder blue.

It’s also Montessori inspired, which means the furniture is scaled to a child’s body so they can climb in and get to work on their own. It’s a splurge, from $469 for a table and one chair up to $999 for four chairs. But it’s handsome enough that you won’t mind it in the living room or kitchen. It’s available for preorder. It’s designed for ages 3 to 6.

Small Beads, Big Calm
Super Smalls, Make It Yummy Mini Bead Kit, $22

There’s something very soothing about threading beads onto a string, one at a time. Super Smalls, founded by the former fashion magazine editor Maria Dueñas Jacobs, makes some of the most charming bead kits around. My favorite is the Make It Yummy mini kit that comes in a palm-sized box with food-related beads and three charms (an egg, a slice of pizza, and a donut), plus enough stretchy cord for a necklace and a bracelet, or three bracelets. It’s a perfect stocking stuffer.

If food isn’t your thing, it comes in plenty of other themes, including fruit, rainbows, ocean, outer space, and a Make It Mazel version with Jewish charms like a chai and a hamsa. Kids who catch the bug can graduate to the Super Entrepreneur Bead Kit ($75), which has more than 630 beads, 25-plus charms, and jewelry cards and stands so they can set up their own shop. Designed for ages 3 and up.

Screen Free Gaming
Tonies, Tonieplay Games, $24.99 each; Tonieplay Controller, $14.99 (requires Toniebox 2, from $139.99)

The Toniebox, the beloved cube that plays stories when kids set a figurine on top, has a new trick. The latest version of the device allows kids to play screen-free games. Thanks to clever design, the games operate on audio commands and a small dial-shaped controller that allows kids to make choices or select answers.

This year, Tonies teamed up with Hasbro to create audio versions of three classics: The Game of Life, Guess Who? and Monopoly. Kids can play by themselves or with others.

The Book That Reads Along
Cali, Cali Reader + 3 Stories, $99

Cali Reader looks and feels like a real book but, like magic, it reads stories aloud to kids. The child begins by snapping a 32-page paper storybook (like The Three Little Pigs or Winnie-the-Pooh) into the reader and pressing the pages to hear the story read aloud as they follow along. Each book comes with three games and word-recognition activities designed by educators, so it can help children build reading skills. In a small pilot study, first graders who used it made bigger gains in phonics, fluency, and vocabulary than a control group. Designed for ages 3 to 6.

Lights Out, Story On
Yoto, Yoto Player 4th Gen, $149.99

The Yoto has become a fixture of the screen-free bedroom, and this fall the company released a major upgrade. Kids still pop in cards to play audiobooks, music, and podcasts. But a new Green Button lets them operate a custom playlist, like a morning music mix or a bedtime wind-down, without having to plug in a particular card. There’s also a new full-panel night light that glows in seven colors and doubles as an OK-to-wake light. The player holds more than 1,000 hours of audio for offline listening. For kids on the go, the smaller Yoto Mini 4th Gen ($109.99) is now splash- and dust-resistant. Designed for ages 3 and up.

#10397. How to Improve Email Deliverability Rates

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

You wrote a good email. You hit send. Then half your list never saw it, because it went straight to spam.

That is a deliverability problem, and it costs more than most teams think. Every email that misses the inbox is a lead you paid for and never reached.

The good part is that deliverability is not luck. Mailbox providers like Gmail, Yahoo and Outlook judge you on a short list of things: who you are, who you send to, and how people react. Fix those and your inbox placement goes up.

This guide covers 10 email deliverability best practices in the order you should fix them, starting with SPF and ending with sender reputation.

Email deliverability is the share of your emails that land in the inbox instead of the spam folder or nowhere at all.

People often mix it up with delivery rate. They are not the same thing.

You can have a 99% delivery rate and still have most of your emails sitting in spam. That is why your email tool can say "delivered" while your open rate keeps dropping.

The big mailbox providers stopped treating authentication as optional.

Microsoft followed on May 5, 2025. If you send more than 5,000 emails a day to Outlook.com, Hotmail or Live addresses, you need all three records in place or your mail goes to junk.

Send less than 5,000 a day? Follow the rules anyway. The same checks decide inbox placement for small senders too, just without the public warning.

SPF (Sender Policy Framework) is a TXT record in your DNS. It lists the servers allowed to send email from your domain.

When your email arrives, the receiving server checks that list. If the sending server is not on it, the email looks suspicious.

DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) adds a digital signature to each email. The receiving server uses a public key in your DNS to check two things: the email came from you, and nobody changed it on the way.

Your email provider gives you the DKIM record. You paste it into your DNS and switch signing on.

DKIM also survives forwarding, which SPF does not. If you can only get one of the two perfect, get DKIM right.

DMARC ties SPF and DKIM together. It tells mailbox providers what to do when an email fails both checks, and it sends you reports on who is sending mail under your domain name.

p=none means "take no action, just send me reports." It is the minimum Gmail, Yahoo and Microsoft accept from bulk senders.

Don't stop there. Read the reports for a few weeks, fix any real sender that is failing, then move up:

One more thing: DMARC needs alignment. The domain in your From address has to match the domain used in SPF or DKIM. Plenty of senders have all three records and still fail DMARC because their email tool signs with its own domain.

If you'd rather not handle this in-house, you can also hire a B2B cold email marketing agency such as IntentSignal, Martal or Belkins. A good agency will set up the domains, mailboxes, warm-up and SPF, DKIM and DMARC records for you, and keep an eye on deliverability while the campaigns run.

A new domain has no history. If it sends 10,000 emails on day one, it looks exactly like a spammer who just bought a domain.

Warm-up means starting small and growing a little each day, so mailbox providers can watch how people react to you.

Send to your most active contacts first. Their opens and replies are what build trust early. If bounces or complaints jump, hold at that volume until they settle.

And if you run cold outreach, do it from a separate domain or subdomain. That way a bad campaign can't hurt the domain your invoices and password resets come from.

A bigger list is not a better list. Dead addresses and people who stopped caring pull your numbers down.

Never buy a list. Bought lists are full of spam traps, which are addresses that exist only to catch senders who email people without permission. Hitting a few of them can get your domain blocklisted.

Yes, you lose some sign-ups. What you keep is real people with working inboxes who actually want your emails. That means fewer bounces, fewer complaints and better opens from day one.

It also keeps bots and fake addresses out of your forms, which matters a lot if your sign-up form is public.

Most email platforms add these for you. Check that yours does.

These two numbers tell you the most about where you stand.

The complaint figures come from Gmail's own rules. The bounce figures are the working limits most email platforms use.

A 0.3% complaint rate is only 3 complaints per 1,000 emails. It does not take much to cross that line.

If complaints are climbing, ask three questions:

Most complaint problems come from one of those three, not from the email itself.

Spam filters got smarter. A single word like "free" won't sink you anymore. Patterns will.

Replies help a lot. When someone replies, the mailbox provider sees a real conversation. Ask a question in your welcome email and you'll get some.

Sender reputation is the score mailbox providers give your domain and IP. Everything above feeds into it. A good score means inbox. A bad one means spam, no matter how good the email is.

You can't see the exact score, but these free tools get you close:

Check them weekly, and right after any big campaign.

A few habits protect your reputation over time:

Aim for 95% or higher inbox placement. Below 90% means something needs fixing, usually authentication or list quality.

The common causes are missing or broken SPF, DKIM or DMARC records, a high complaint rate, an old list with lots of dead addresses, or a new domain that sent too much too soon. Check authentication first because it is the fastest to fix.

DNS fixes like SPF and DKIM take effect within a day or two. Reputation is slower. Expect two to six weeks of steady, clean sending before inbox placement recovers.

Yes. The 5,000 mark is where Gmail, Yahoo and Microsoft start enforcing openly. Small senders are still judged on the same signals, and Gmail asks every sender for at least SPF or DKIM.

Only if you send enough to keep it warm, roughly 100,000 emails a month or more. Below that, a good shared IP from a trusted provider usually performs better.

Sender reputation covers both your IP address and your domain. Domain reputation is the part tied to your domain name, and it follows you even if you switch email providers. Gmail leans on domain reputation more than IP.

If you only have an hour this week, spend it on SPF, DKIM and DMARC. Nothing else works until those pass.

After that, clean your list and keep an eye on complaints. Send emails people asked for, to people who still want them, from a domain that proves who it is. Do that for a few weeks and your emails will land in the inbox again.

#10396. Save serious money with RedPocket Mobile’s $5 Black Friday plans

You’re not going to believe this, but there’s one part of your life that’s not actually getting more expensive. If you switch to RedPocket Mobile during its Black Friday sale, you can ditch your costly carrier and get a plan that starts at $5 per month. It’s not too good to be true: RedPocket has been around for 20 years, and unlike most MVNOs, it’s independently owned and operated. That gives it the ability to offer you real network choice when you sign up for a new plan (we’ll explain more later), and keeps your costs low. Really low.

But you’re reading this on 9to5Google, so how does it impact you as an Android user? That’s a great question.

RedPocket is offering $150 rebates on Android devices like the Pixel 11, Galaxy S26, Galaxy Z Flip 7, Moto G Play, and more. (You can also get $100 rebates for iPhones if you’re into that sort of thing.)

These offers run from November 9 through the 30th at redpocket.com, so don’t wait too long to save big.

It’s OK if you haven’t heard of RedPocket Mobile, because it has been quietly working for 20 years to improve the way people use their phones. Founded in 2006, the company works with all three major US carriers — AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon — and because it doesn’t own any of its towers, it can pass along significant savings to its customers. Here’s what the company says on its website:

RedPocket was built for price-conscious consumers who want real value and freedom from rigid, high-cost contracts. As a no-contract carrier, we’ve stayed focused on making reliable, transparent, and flexible phone service for everyone. Our plans are designed to fit real lifestyles, whether you’re a heavy data user, a frequent traveler, or just looking to cut your monthly bill.

Most MVNOs are owned by the Big Three, which means you don’t really have a choice of network when you sign up. But RedPocket works with all three major carriers and lets you choose which one works best for your location and usage patterns.

RedPocket offers a tool called CoverageGenius that helps you decide which network is right for you. While you can’t switch between networks once your line is set up, it’s a great way to figure out where to start.

I teased that $5/month cost at the beginning of the article, but here’s the real breakdown: you can get a full year of service for $60 if you’re a light data user. RedPocket’s Annual Essentials and Annual Plus plans get you unlimited calling and texting in the US, along with calling and data roaming in dozens of countries around the world. The main difference is how much data you get: 3GB for Essentials and 20GB for Plus.

Annual Premium ups the ante to unlimited data, plus calling and data roaming in even more countries.

Across all three plans, you’re saving between 33% and 50% off the regular price when you sign up between November 9th and 30th.

I even made you a table to make it easier to understand: 👇

One thing to note about all of these plans: the annual prices are paid upfront, not billed monthly. Promotional pricing applies to the first year, and after that, annual plans renew at $110 for Essentials, $220 for Plus, and $330 for Premium.

RedPocket understands that it may be hard to commit to a full year of service even if it’s super cheap. That’s why it offers monthly plans, too, that can serve as a trial for any of the networks. It costs just $10 for the first month to try any of the three plans, with Monthly Plus rising to $20/month after that and Premium $30/month thereafter (Essentials stays at $10/month).

If you need a new phone to go along with your new plan, RedPocket is a great place to get it.

During the Black Friday deal period, you can get a $150 rebate on the following phones:

Legal stuff: Rebates are paid out 90 days after service begins on a new line activation with an eligible plan. Full rebate terms at redpocket.com/rebate. Devices are available while supplies last.

Usually with sponsored content, I have to spend the whole time convincing you that the product is worth buying. But RedPocket’s Black Friday deals do all that work on their own.

Not only do you get amazing discounts for the first 12 months of service by prepaying for a full year, but RedPocket’s “Lock-in Low” promise means that you get to stay as close to that promotional price as possible once the first year is over.

There’s no contract and no port-in requirement. You can keep your number, keep your phone, and activate with an eSIM on compatible devices. During the event, there’s even a Refer-a-Friend credit that gets you $25 for every person you bring to the service.

Explore RedPocket’s plans or compare the annual offers. This is one of the best Black Friday decisions you’re going to make this month, and maybe even ever.

#10394. This farming game is designed to keep you off your phone

There’s one way to win the smartphone game Island: Screen Time Control. You have to stay off your phone. The makers of the gamified screen time blocker are betting that a different approach to smartphone time management can yield better long-term results.

The goal of Island: Screen Time Control is growing virtual crops to sell for digital coins. Crops grow over time, and you can sell them to a boat that arrives once a day. With more money, you can begin to upgrade your island with new crops, trees, flowers, and other features.

The founders of SideKit, which made the app, say the typical approach of nannying screen time or adding friction doesn’t really work. “Most screen time apps use a formula of set limits and a wall that shows up when you exceed them,” SideKit CEO Ashish Selvaraj tells Fast Company. That friction doesn’t change habits, Selvaraj says.

“We believe that there is no level of wall ‘hardness’ that can change your behavior long term,” he says. “As long as you outsource your self-regulation, you won’t be able to see lasting change.”

For their app, Selvaraj and SideKit CTO Ethan Pronev, who met while attending the University of Waterloo in Ontario, Canada, took inspiration from idle games and their most addictive UI features.

The app begins with an onboarding process that asks you to remember the last short-form video you watched and the last time you closed your phone and felt like it was time well spent. From there, you’re taken to your island, a tiny plot of land where you start with 50 coins (cucumbers, for example, cost 20 coins to plant).

You’re asked to share your screen time, then set your own limits for your selected app categories. A screen time bar on the left side of the game shows how close you’ve come to hitting a limit. The more you stick to your time limits, the better the weather is on your island, which creates a bigger harvest.

Instead of logging into your problem apps, you can log into the game and check how your crops are doing and harvest them when they’re ready. The gamified aspect provides a dopamine hit you might get from TikTok or Instagram notifications or infinite scroll, and there are other built-in features that reward you for keeping your limits—but not so many that you’ll spend too much time in the app.

A focus timer is built into a boat offshore that you can click to turn your phone into a timer; it catches fish the longer you’re on it. A credit system improves your credit score every day that you stick to your limits, giving the app its own streak-tracking feature.

The app is free, but there’s a pro subscription for $5.99 per month or $39.99 per year that gives you access to features such as per-app time limits and “soul link” mode, so you and a friend can keep each other even more accountable as both islands suffer if one of you spends too much time on your phone.

The approach is carrot over stick, using positive reinforcement instead of nagging to encourage users to engage in behaviors that help their island and crops. SideKit says it’s working: Over the 18,400 days of data the company has, it says users stopped at or below their set limit 82% of the time.

“Who doesn’t love a farming game?” Selvaraj says.

One of the first partner brands selling Android XR glasses, “Intelligent Eyewear” as Google calls it, has already completely sold out, with Gentle Monster no longer accepting pre-orders just days after launch.

Google’s Gemini-powered Intelligent Eyewear lineup launched last week with collections from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, with pricing starting at $395. Just a few days later, though, over half of the lineup is sold out.

Every single Intelligent Eyewear style from Gentle Monster is currently sold out, with pre-orders no longer available.

Warby Parker, meanwhile, still has most styles fully in stock. Some are delayed, mainly “Reid” which has the wide fit delayed as far as December 28, but others are still shipping on launch day.

#10391. How the Supreme Court’s college admissions decision has changed the job pipeline for Black and Latino students

Jamila Chambers remembers when recruiters came to interview students at Occidental College with a clear mission: They wanted a diverse workforce.

They interviewed juniors for internships that often led to full-time offers. Finance firms came and ran affinity information sessions and job shadowing programs for first- and second-year students.

“They would specifically say: ‘We’re looking for BIPOC students. We’re looking for first-gen students. We’re looking for LGBTQIA+ students,’” said Chambers, executive director of the school’s Hameetman Career Center.

Not anymore. Those pipelines, Chambers said, have “dried up.” 

After a divided Supreme Court gutted race-conscious admissions in 2023, colleges could no longer give an edge to Black and Latino applicants over white and Asian applicants in the name of diversity, ushering in a new era for higher education. That meant the end of policies aimed at turning around historically low representation and systemic discrimination. 

The court’s ruling—which more than two-thirds of American adults told Gallup was “mostly a good thing”—did not address or change hiring laws nor mention employer efforts to make workplaces more inclusive.

Yet many employers have since dismantled existing efforts to recruit diverse workers on college campuses, reporting by The Hechinger Report and Soledad O’Brien Productions found. 

Company leaders removed or revised diversity language, changed recruitment strategies and reconsidered how they built pools of candidates, according to a Columbia Business School study based on a survey of human resources professionals. Half of those surveyed who were familiar with the ruling mistakenly believed it applied to workplaces; others feared becoming a target of lawsuits, public criticism, or political attention.

They’re facing a hostile atmosphere. In January 2025, as one of the first acts of his second term, President Donald Trump issued an executive order that attacked so-called diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) hiring programs across federal agencies and contractors.

Calling these efforts “discriminatory and illegal,” the order also pressured private employers to follow suit—including publicly traded corporations, large nonprofits, and universities with big endowments.   

Fear of drawing Trump’s ire appears to be the major reason many private employers have removed racial and gender representation goals from their hiring pipelines. Conservative legal activists used the Supreme Court ruling on affirmative action at colleges as a road map for targeting workplace programs that prioritize diversity. 

The Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank, urged businesses to remove or revoke corporate DEI positions, warning state and federal governments not to contract with corporations that have such statements. 

The full impact the ban on affirmative action at colleges will have on job placement won’t be known until 2028, once the first class of college students admitted since the decision graduates and enters the workforce. But one of the starkest consequences of both the court ruling and the pressures of the second Trump administration is already clear, as colleges and workplaces alike retreated from promises to fight racism and injustice through bolstered diversity programs that they made after the 2020 murder of George Floyd by a Minneapolis police officer. 

“I feel like this is clearly a backlash to that moment,” said Natasha Warikoo, a sociology professor at Tufts University who has studied affirmative action, noting that previously, a focus on racial justice “felt like a moral imperative.”

Bryan J. Cook, director of higher education policy in the Work, Education, and Labor Division at the Urban Institute, said what he sees so far in early workforce trends is concerning, although he added that the midterm election’s sweeping verdict on Trump “could have some impact.” With Democrats controlling the House and Senate, he said, “It will be interesting to see if Congress pushes back on the administration’s anti-DEI efforts, including some to the DOJ investigations into schools’ admissions practices.”

More than three dozen major companies contacted for this story—among them Meta, Google, Walmart, Target and Goldman Sachs—declined to discuss their recruiting practices, a stark contrast to companies’ previously publicized efforts to diversify their workforces.

In addition, dozens of colleges approached for interviews would not make their career staff available or did not respond. Several counselors agreed to talk only if neither they nor their schools were named, citing concern about drawing the attention of the Trump administration.

Following the court’s decision, Black enrollment declined or remained flat at nearly all highly selective private and public colleges—the 85 that accept 25% or less of applicants—and the same was true of Hispanic enrollment at more than half of those institutions. 

For example, at Harvard University, one of the defendants in the Supreme Court case, the percentage of incoming students who are Black has fallen by nearly half since 2023. That year, they made up 18% of the first-year class, while in 2026, they’re just 9.3%. 

Meanwhile, the path to the most prestigious entry-level jobs is also narrowing to favor students from a smaller set of largely private elite colleges—places where the entering classes are becoming less diverse, said Matt Sigelman, president of The Burning Glass Institute, a labor research firm.  

Before the decision, when companies and recruiters had broader diversity goals, they were casting a wider net, Sigelman said. And though the court decision was about college admissions, employers “could see the writing on the wall and changed the way they were hiring.”

They put together guidance they were getting from the Department of Labor along with changes in the political culture, said Sigelman, and “in many cases pulled back from their diversity goals.’’

Burning Glass looked at the careers of 300,000 college graduates who entered the workforce between 2023 and 2025 to understand who landed where, and specifically who got jobs at the most competitive companies. 

Over that period, the share of those hires coming from the most elite colleges rose by nearly a third, according to the firm’s research, which typically draws on large databases of online career profiles, such as those on LinkedIn, and job postings. 

The results suggest that landing a good first job increasingly depends on which college a student gets into, and Sigelman thinks first-generation and minority students will remain at a particular disadvantage if they aren’t already known to employers.

“What started as a decision about who gets admitted to college ultimately plays out in who gets a shot at the best employment,” Sigelman said.

Other research on recruiting points yields similar findings. While nearly 60% of 150 major employers identified diversity as a priority for determining where to send campus recruiters in 2022, that figure was down to 31% in 2025, according to a survey by Veris Insights, a recruiting research firm. Over the same period, the share of major companies recruiting exclusively from a short list of schools rose from 17% to 26%, the survey found.

There are also early signs that internships—an important employment pipeline for college students—are becoming more difficult for minority students to obtain, according to the National Association of Colleges and Employers, which connects college career offices with the employers that recruit from them.

The association tracks the makeup of corporate internship programs, one of the main pipelines that companies used to diversify their workforce. It found that from 2021 to 2024, white students made up 50% to 53% of those interns. 

In the cohort that ran from fall 2024 through summer 2025, spanning Trump’s return to office, that share rose to 59%, said Shawn VanDerziel, the association’s president and CEO. He added that the weak job market, artificial intelligence, and inflation make it difficult to interpret this trend. 

California had already banned race-based affirmative action in public university admissions in 1996, with lasting consequences for students’ education and economic prospects, studies found. Still, recruiters regularly visited California’s campuses seeking out students of color, first-generation students, and women in science and engineering.

But now, at the University of California, Berkeley, Santina Pitcher, senior associate director of employer relations, said federal agencies “from the Peace Corps to the State Department” have told her they can no longer explicitly recruit for diversity.

Recruiters “weren’t approaching us in the same way” at Pomona College after the court ruling, said Hazel Raja, associate dean and senior director of the career development office on the private campus in Claremont, California.

“My assumption is that there was a little bit of everybody pulling back to begin with, and then reassessing ways that they could still diversify their workforce in ways that still allowed for them to stay above the law in light of the policy changes,” Raja said.

At San Jose State University, where more than 40% of students are the first in their families to attend college, the career center renamed some programs soon after the federal government changed its guidance in response to Trump’s executive order. References to DEI disappeared. 

What was once called a diversity job fair has been renamed the October Fest job and internship fair, said Lisa Trikofski, assistant director of employment engagement at the campus career center.

Students say they can feel a shift underway.  

At San Jose State last spring, students moved through a career fair with résumés and rehearsed handshakes, navigating booths for companies that were looking to recruit. Winnie Tuban, who is Filipino and first in her family to go to college, said she enrolled at the school because it sits at the center of the design world she wanted to enter in Silicon Valley, close to headquarters for several tech company giants. 

Apple, Google, Meta, Adobe and Zoom recruited San Jose State graduates over the years and hired scores of them. Tuban has since graduated and ultimately found a job at a small startup in San Francisco on her own, not through recruiters.

She said she found the landscape discouraging. “I feel like regardless of where you stand politically, when you’re living as a person of color and you hear that they’re ‘going to war on DEI,’ it makes it feel like you’re not welcome in that space,” she said.

Daniella Mensah, a psychology major, was 2 when her family immigrated from Ghana. Her father works in government and her mother is a hairdresser, and she worries that students like her—people of color looking for their first job—are increasingly being overlooked because of policy changes.

“I think a lot of companies don’t feel the need to work hard to allow other people of different backgrounds into those positions,” Mensah said. “It feels like an afterthought,” she added. “I think that has definitely affected the population entering those roles.” 

There are many who believe that giving preferences to students like Mensah for both college admissions and jobs based on their identity is just wrong, including Frederick Hess, director of education policy studies at the American Enterprise Institute, a conservative think tank in Washington, D.C.

That idea, Hess said, “far too often seems to have been reduced to counting the number of people from a particular race or ethnic group.” 

In his view, real diversity would also mean hiring people from different regions, social classes, religions, and political outlooks. “Businesses can’t pretend that selecting employees based on skin color is a good proxy for all of the rich differences that they say they want to attend to,” he said.

Back at Occidental College, Chambers, who is Black and in her 50s, worries her students are entering a job market where the legal and policy protections she relied on early in her career are being stripped away.

In her office, she keeps a picture of the civil rights activist Ruby Bridges, who was 6 when she integrated an all-white elementary school in New Orleans in 1960. 

Bridges did that “so I can work in higher ed,” Chambers said. 

Now, she is having conversations with her own children that echo the conversations her parents had with her, in a very different era.

“It is a challenge,” she said. “But we’re up for it.”

This story was produced by The Hechinger Report, a nonprofit, independent news organization focused on inequality and innovation in education.

Liz Willen and Maxine Paul Emile contributed reporting to this story about the end of affirmative action. It’s the third in a series of articles accompanying a documentary produced by a partnership between The Hechinger Report and  Soledad O’Brien Productions, about the ongoing impact of the Supreme Court ruling. #10389. The price of success nobody warns founders about: Who are you after you sell your company?

We entrepreneurs spend decades learning how to build, scale, and exit successful businesses, and there are countless books, podcasts, courses, and articles dedicated to the pursuit of this goal.

Yet almost nobody teaches us how to live after the exit.

In 2008, I did what most entrepreneurs dream of doing. I exited the business I’d spent nearly two decades building, just before the global financial crisis. By almost any measure, it was a remarkable success.

What I discovered, and what I want to share with my fellow entrepreneurs, is that no one tells you about the psychological consequences of success. We celebrate the exit as the ultimate achievement: the culmination of years of sacrifice, sleepless nights, and relentless determination. A liquidity event takes place and the founder collects the check and disappears into a life of freedom and fulfilment. That’s the narrative, anyway.

But my experience was very different, because my identity was fully linked to my business and everything it represented. I didn’t recognize it then, but I’d confused what I did with who I was. Without the business, I wasn’t entirely sure who I was anymore, and almost overnight my identity disappeared.

What I’ve come to find out is that this is much more common than you may think it is.

The hidden cost of no exit plan

I built my property advisory business, Ober-Haus, after arriving in Estonia in the early 1990s, and developed it into a company that operated across seven countries. For nearly 20 years, my life revolved around building, negotiating, financing, and solving problems. I loved it and became good at it.

Then I sold the company. Suddenly, I had the financial freedom I’d only dreamed about and spent most of my adult life pursuing—but that was when things began to unravel. Years before building Ober-Haus, I’d confronted alcoholism, entered recovery, and rebuilt my life. Yet I hadn’t fully recognized how easily the compulsive drive that once fueled my drinking could find a more socially celebrated outlet: ambition and success.

After my exit, I moved to Argentina and immersed myself in a world of horses, polo, travel, and an extraordinary lifestyle. From the outside, it looked like the perfect reward for decades of hard work. Parts of it were wonderful, but something fundamental was missing.

I’d spent so long pursuing financial independence that I hadn’t seriously considered what I would do with it once I had it. The adrenaline of building a business had been replaced by the pleasures of spending the proceeds. What I mistook for freedom was, in some ways, another form of escape. And the purpose of life disappeared slowly until finally it was gone.

Over time, my wealth diminished. My marriage collapsed. I made difficult financial decisions and watched much of what I’d accumulated disappear. The exit that was supposed to secure my future became the beginning of one of the most difficult periods of my life, and came with a hidden cost that I’d never considered.

A darker side to success

Looking back, I can see that the problem began long before I sold my company.

Entrepreneurs develop qualities that help us succeed: drive, competitiveness, resilience, an appetite for risk, and an almost obsessive determination to achieve our goals. These characteristics can build extraordinary businesses, but they don’t necessarily build extraordinary lives.

We become accustomed to controlling outcomes, solving problems and measuring progress. We approach relationships like negotiations and personal fulfilment like another business objective. When something isn’t working, our instinct is to push harder or cut our losses. Success demands sacrifice; we accept that almost without thinking, whether it’s another missed family dinner, another canceled holiday, or another year promising ourselves that life will slow down after the next transaction.

But there comes a moment when success starts asking for something we’re no longer willing to give. Our health. Our integrity. Our relationships. Perhaps even our sense of self. And the question becomes whether we can keep going without betraying ourselves further.

This is the dark side of success that is rarely discussed—the problem with getting everything we ever wanted. Not because entrepreneurs don’t experience it, but because admitting it feels dangerously close to admitting failure.

The answer isn’t another achievement

When my life began falling apart, my instinct was familiar: start another business. I’ve done just that with a property credit business in the U.K., which restored direction, confidence, and financial purpose.

What’s different this time around, however, is that I’ve come to understand that rebuilding a business and rebuilding a life are two different things. One can be measured in revenues, assets and returns. The other requires questions that don’t fit neatly into a spreadsheet: Who am I without the title? What do I actually want? Which relationships have I neglected? What am I still trying to prove, and to whom?

These are uncomfortable questions for people accustomed to having answers, which is how many entrepreneurs operate. Yet avoiding them simply postpones the reckoning.

It’s been hard to face this, especially when you consider that we live in a culture obsessed with optimization. We’re encouraged to extend our peak, maximize performance, preserve our youth, and constantly reinvent ourselves. While there’s nothing inherently wrong with that, sometimes this optimization becomes a sophisticated way of avoiding harder questions about identity, relationships, integrity and purpose.

A changed relationship with success

I want to share my story because I suspect there are thousands of successful founders wrestling with the question of who they are after the exit. From the outside, they appear to have everything. Inside, they’re wondering what happened.

Today, in my sixties, I’m still an entrepreneur, still ambitious, and still interested in creating things. But the fundamental difference this time around is that my relationship with success has changed. I’m beginning to understand that my next chapter isn’t necessarily about becoming the version of the person I used to be—it’s about letting go of the person I no longer need to be.

Contrary to what all the books and courses and stories tell you, the hardest part of success isn’t reaching the top. It’s actually when you discover that the person you became to get there is no longer the person you want to be.

So if you’re an entrepreneur in a similar position, I invite you to consider the idea that your identity is more than your business achievements, and to then find the courage to build a life that doesn’t require you to keep climbing.

#10388. Someone rebuilt old Android versions in your browser, and it’s an instant nostalgia hit [Gallery]

The “Android Time Machine” is a fun project that puts Android versions into your browser, giving you a quick and easy chance to play around with older versions for a quick hit of nostalgia.

Built on the back of AOSP builds for classic Nexus devices, “Android Time Machine” lets you quickly access older Android versions. Specifically, Android 2.1 Eclair through Android 7.1.2 Nougat.

The simulator runs within the shell of a matching Nexus smartphone on a desktop browser, or to fit your actual smartphone if you run it on Android.

Versions and simulated smartphones include:

The best part here is how it works on your actual smartphone. When launched in fullscreen, it scales to match your phone’s screen – meaning it fits even devices like the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s smaller outer display (it just shows the desktop version when open).

Since this is running through the browser and not an actual Android build, you won’t get a perfect replication. Performance is a little hit or miss, especially with certain animations, but it works really well overall.

The browser even simulates results from each era (oh, to go back to when Google Search wasn’t an absolute mess). Similarly, Google apps and the camera are filled with placeholders since the web app can’t access the actual camera or connect to the internet to sign into a Google account.

Seeing things like the boot animations and live wallpapers from classic Nexus phones, as well as peeking back at lost apps like Google+ and Play Music, is just such a fun little piece of nostalgia.

“Android Time Machine” is free, and the source code is available on GitHub.

#10387. How to Use IP Geolocation to Stop Bots and Fraud (Without Hurting UX)

Several methods can help you deal with online threats and strengthen security. All are effective, but each has a trade-off. For example, the harder you make it for bots to affect your website’s performance, the more likely you are to frustrate real customers.

Those of you who browse online daily know that credential stuffing, fake signups & payment fraud keep growing. To prevent fraud, businesses install CAPTCHAs & hard blocks that treat bots and legitimate users the same, diverting them to your competitors.

IP geolocation maps an IP address to a physical location & network details, letting you spot suspicious traffic before it reaches sensitive actions. Used well, it’s an invisible, low-friction risk signal. In this guide, you will learn how to flag high-risk activity and apply soft geo-fencing with step-up authentication.

Today, an IP lookup returns far more than a country & city. It can also reveal several other parameters, like

Each of these fields acts as a clue telling who is really behind a request.

This data powers anomaly detection. You can start by building a baseline for normal behavior for each user with aspects like

Then, you can watch for deviations from that pattern. An attacker won’t look like the account’s real owner, so you'll catch them.

Geolocation makes several common attack patterns easy to spot:

The first is traffic bursts from data center ASNs. These are bots, as real customers don’t browse from cloud servers

Many accounts created from one IP or subnet. This is a clear sign of fake signups

Impossible travel, such as logins from two distant locations within minutes

Timezone vs. IP mismatch. A device’s clock disagrees with its apparent location.

Note: Geolocation is just a signal, not a verdict. VPNs, travel, & mobile carriers can all create false alarms, so it works best when combined with other signals. That’s exactly why a proportional, soft response beats a hard block.

In short, IP geolocation turns a bare IP address into context, helping you separate real users from automated or fraudulent traffic.

Not every IP geolocation anomaly deserves the same response. The simplest way to stay consistent is to define a clear risk-signal framework.

That can be a short list of checks. Each check can have a weight that reflects how strongly it suggests fraud.

With risk scoring, you can turn these checks into a decision. You just have to assign each signal a numeric weight.

For example, medium can be 10 & 30 can be high.

Now, you need to add up every signal that comes up & map the total to thresholds like

A single medium signal passes quietly, but several can trigger action.

If you treat this as an automatic block, it would punish legitimate customers. Instead, let it raise the score & you take action only if it stacks with other signals, like a hosting IP or a new device.

Now that you know how to quantify the risk, here is how you can protect yourself without damaging UX.

Before soft, let us learn about hard blocking. This is where you completely deny or permanently ban traffic from specific geographic regions.

Now, hard blocking by country may look effective, but it can backfire quickly. Here is how.

In the worst case, determined bot operators simply rotate to IPs in allowed regions, so the only people you stop are your real customers.

This is where the balance between security and user experience becomes critical. As the digital strategist and Founder at LawRank, Mariano Rodriguez emphasizes, "Your website's security should be a silent guardian, not a roadblock. If your fraud prevention creates friction, you aren't just stopping bots—you're turning away real clients. True digital trust is built when backend protections are seamless and invisible to the legitimate user."

Now, with soft geo-fencing, you can respond to risk proportionally instead of making a simple allow-or-deny call. Instead of totally banning the users, you adjust the level of friction to match the risk score from the previous section:

**Note: **For soft geo-fencing, passkeys are safest because they are phishing-resistant. Only a legitimate user can take the biometric tap and pass.

Before we start, let’s understand Express.js middleware. An Express.js middleware for Geolocation Risk Scores is a custom or 3rd party function that intercepts the incoming HTTP requests, extracts the client's IP address, fetches a security risk profile based on their geographic location & attaches that data to the request object (req) before it reaches your route handlers.

Here is how you can use it for fraud prevention and bot mitigation:

Note: You can make it stronger by adding velocity checks (too many attempts from one IP or account) & device fingerprints.

From a broader angle, IP geolocation isn't the final verdict. It is just a signal. But with this signal, you can score each request, respond in proportion to the risk & save hard blocks for clear abuse. This increases the friction for bots and keeps the flow easy for legitimate users.
