Our enterprise and data center SSD reviews show how a drive performs in real-world service, not just on its best day.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After a hiatus of several years, Tom's Hardware is expanding its in-depth testing and analysis to enterprise and data center SSDs. Consumer SSDs and conventional hard drives lack the performance and endurance for extensive AI workloads. This has increased demand for enterprise SSDs. Form factors like U.2, U.3, E3.S, and E1.S, once rare, are now common in high-end workstations and home labs. These enterprise storage solutions provide higher capacities, better performance, and greater reliability than consumer drives.

Comprehensive reviews of enterprise and data center SSDs are therefore more important than ever. Buying a drive of this caliber is a major decision and a significant investment for organizations of all sizes. With this latest venture, Tom's Hardware will continue to help buyers make informed decisions with comprehensive reviews and performance analyses.

Reviewing enterprise and data center SSDs required us to build a workstation that could truly challenge these drives. This project would not have been possible without the support of several component makers, including Asus, Corsair, G.Skill, Icy Dock, and Noctua, who made the workstation a reality, a challenging prospect in the current market.

The Xeon 658X, a 24-core, 48-thread chip from the Granite Rapids family with a 4.9 GHz boost clock speed, powers the testing workstation. Single-core performance and total core count matter just as much when reviewing storage. Clock speed determines how many IOPS one core can push and how fast it answers a single request, while 24 cores let us spread a drive's load across eight fio jobs and later test several drives at once. The Xeon 658X ticks all those boxes.

We've entrusted the Xeon 658X's cooling to Noctua's NH-U14S DX-4677 air cooler, which supports both LGA4677 and LGA4710 sockets. The single-tower CPU air cooler delivers high-performance cooling at very low noise levels thanks to its dual NF-A15 140mm cooling fans.

With its server-grade components and robust enterprise features, the Asus Pro WS W890E-Sage SE is the ideal motherboard to pair with the Xeon 658X. Its extensive feature set includes an onboard MCIO x8 connection, split into x4/x4, that allows for evaluating two U.2 or U.3 drives. The board also provides seven PCIe 5.0 expansion slots (six at x16 and one at x8) to fully leverage the Xeon 658X’s 128 PCIe 5.0 lanes, so the SSDs and graphics cards never hit bandwidth limits.

We're still in need of support for an RTX Pro graphics card, which would be an invaluable asset for enterprise SSD reviews for real-world AI workloads, but our current test platform allows us to test the most important aspects of performance.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Despite the memory and storage shortage, G.Skill and Corsair have stepped up to provide crucial components for our enterprise SSD test bench. G.Skill sent a G5 DDR5-6400 C32 64GB (4x16GB) R-DIMM memory kit, which runs at the stock DDR5-5600 speed. The decision to keep it at the JEDEC baseline has nothing to do with the memory kit: Memory frequency does not affect performance in enterprise SSD tests.

Meanwhile, Corsair provided the speedy MP700 Pro XT 2TB, one of the best SSDs, as the test bench's primary storage. The PCIe 5.0 drive delivers sequential read and write speeds up to 14,900 MB/s and 14,500 MB/s, respectively, and keeps the workstation snappy, especially when it hammers enterprise drives all day long.

No power supply is better suited to the job than the Corsair HX1500i. It offers a massive 1,500W capacity with plenty of headroom for future upgrades, and it runs quietly and stably, two qualities that matter when you keep the test system running for countless hours. It is an 80 Plus Platinum power supply with at least 89% efficiency at full load.

Testing enterprise drives in a standard PCIe expansion slot is more convenient. For that purpose, Icy Dock has provided us with the ExpressSlot Elite MB221E5P-B and MB303E5P-B to accept one and two E1.S SSDs. Unlike other generic designs on the market, these adapters feature tool-less installation mechanisms that don't require removing them from the PCIe expansion slot, and they include 50mm fans for active cooling.

The list also included the ToughArmor MB218E5P-B, a 5.25-inch drive bay that supports up to eight E1.S SSDs for future projects exploring RAID arrays. To test E3.S drives, we use a JMT ADT-R27C adapter strapped to a Noctua NF-F12 industrialPPC-24V-3000 IP67 PWM cooling fan, which can run at 12V and still provide substantial airflow to actively cool the SSDs under evaluation.

A TGDGamer E-ATX test bench houses the hardware for the enterprise SSD system. It may not look flashy, but it does the job, and that is what matters. As an open-air test bench, it is easy to install and remove hardware, and it eliminates variables when it comes to heat generation and buildup. The test bench also supports motherboard form factors up to SSI-EEB, so the Asus Pro WS W890E-Sage SE feels right at home.

A spec sheet only tells you what a drive can do on its best day. The real world is not as pretty. The drive is mostly full, garbage collection is constantly at work, and multiple workloads are hitting it simultaneously. Our enterprise benchmark suite is built to measure the drive in service: at steady state, under load, through write bursts, and with other jobs running. Every drive gets the same automated run on the same test bench. Every result is stored with the exact parameters that produced it, so we can trace how we got there.

This can take some time. A full run takes most of a day on a 7.68TB PCIe 5.0 drive, and it writes the drive end-to-end many times over. To make life a bit easier on us, the benchmark can be run unattended, and it’s crash-resumable from the last stage. A shorter express mode handles bench checks and quick triage. When a result looks odd, express runs and variant runs, which repeat just the tests in question or change one setting, help us find the cause before we take it to the vendor.

We run the bench on a custom Debian 13 image that we build and maintain ourselves, with the suite copied in at build time. This image gets installed on the bench’s OS drive, and the kernel is pinned so every drive has the same software stack. Right now that’s Linux 7.2.6 from Debian backports, because Debian 13’s stock 6.12 kernel predates support for the Asus Pro WS W890E-Sage SE’s Intel E610 10GbE controller. The suite is also designed to be run remotely if needed, but we need a tester at the bench to switch the drives, of course.

Debian is our pick over Ubuntu for a few reasons: it has fewer background services, no Snap, and no unattended upgrades by default. We hold the kernel so nothing changes between runs. We remove AppArmor and turn off scheduled jobs that could fire mid-run, like the weekly TRIM timer and the drive-health service that polls every drive, and the suite records any that are still running. The suite also turns off NVMe autonomous power-state transitions (APST) at the start of every run and checks that the drive reports it off, so no drive drops into a low-power state during an idle gap and adds wake-up latency to the next I/O.

Every test runs in fio 3.42, using io_uring and direct I/O against the raw block device. This means no filesystem and no page cache sitting between fio and the drive; the bench’s 64GB of RAM never caches a byte of test data. We compile fio from source because Debian’s packaged version lacks SPRandom, which we’ll get to in short order.

Some enterprise storage reviews run application profiles in Oracle’s Vdbench, but we decided to go full fio. This makes for a more consistent suite with one set of latency accounting across every chart. And fio is open source and actively maintained, while Vdbench hasn’t had a new release since 2018. Vdbench profiles are built from the same parts fio uses, such as read/write ratio, block-size mix, and random or sequential access, and our mixed-workload sweeps cover the common read/write ratios at 4K and 8K, though not mixed-block-size profiles. Running Vdbench ourselves wouldn’t make our results comparable to other outlets’ anyway, since they use different hardware, preconditioning, and profile definitions.

A key element of benchmarking SSDs is making sure the test drive is at steady state, with the performance it can sustain rather than the peak you can see after a fresh erase. Our first stage is a secure erase using nvme format. If a drive refuses, the suite falls back to a plain format, then a full-drive discard, and records which one it used.

Next comes preconditioning. SPRandom, SanDisk’s open-source contribution to fio, is a faster alternative to filling the drive over and over for hours. It takes user capacity and over-provisioning (OP) as inputs, which SanDisk says lets it reach a steady-state layout in just one pass. Overprovisioning (OP) is inferred from the capacity point or given by the tester. NVMe drives don’t report their raw flash, so a 7.68TB drive like our first one, assumed to sit on 8TiB of actual NAND, works out to having about 14.5% OP.

We don’t take SPRandom’s result on faith. A steady-state gate follows, running 4K random writes at queue depth 256 (QD256) until the drive’s write speed stops moving. It uses the two tests from the Storage Networking Industry Association’s (SNIA) steady-state rule, with limits ten times tighter, applied to the last 30 minutes: split into five six-minute rounds, the round averages must sit within 2% of one another, and the trend line across the window can’t move more than 1%.

That takes a while, but that’s the point: an earlier, looser version of the gate passed our first drive while its write speed was still climbing. The whole settling curve is saved with every run, and a drive that doesn’t settle within three hours is marked as not reaching steady state, though the run continues. As a backstop, the suite repeats the four-corner 4K write after the random sweep, hours later, and flags the run if the two results differ by more than 3%.

The suite also checks its own results as it goes. If a test’s slowest moment falls below 70% of its average, that test is run again on the spot. If a point in the random sweep lands more than 10% off the curve set by its neighbors, it’s measured again before the drive is erased for the sequential tests. Both results are kept, and any re-test is noted in the review.

Following the random tests, the tool erases the drive again and writes it end to end once, with 128K sequential writes at QD64. We run it before the sequential and AI tests, so the drive is conditioned with the kind of I/O we’re about to measure. It matters because sequential writes can swing wildly on a randomly written drive: on our first test drive, the fastest result was more than three times the slowest. After a sequential fill, they held flat from QD2 through QD1024, at both 128K and 1MB.

Drives are formatted to 512-byte logical blocks when they support it, so our block size sweep can go down to 512-byte transfers, which a 4K-native namespace can’t issue. SNIA’s enterprise IOPS test uses 512-byte transfers too, and Kioxia pitches 512-byte access for its GP Series, which is aimed at GPU-initiated storage. Drives without a 512-byte format are tested as shipped, and their sub-4K results are marked unsupported. The switch happens in the same format command as the secure erase, so it adds no time.

A fast enough SSD will happily benchmark your host, or your tools, instead, and our early runs turned up three ways that could happen. The first is CPU idle states, or C-states: waking our Xeon 658X cores from their deepest idle state can take up to 170 microseconds, and at QD1 that directly impacts the results. Holding the cores awake for the whole run cut the first drive’s average 4K QD1 read latency by about a sixth.

The second is the CPU itself: a single fio job can saturate its core well short of what a PCIe 5.0 drive can manage. Split across eight jobs, the same test runs several times faster, so random tests now spread their queue depth across up to eight fio jobs. That’s also why fast cores, and enough of them, matter for this test bench.

The third is fio itself. By default, fio seeds its random generator the same way every run, so it replays the same sequence of random offsets, and each random write test rewrites the previous test’s blocks in the same order. On our first drive, that was the main reason 4K random writes came in at more than twice the sustained figure. Every random test now runs with a fresh random seed.

What we don’t change matters, too. Completions arrive by interrupt rather than polling, and the IOMMU stays in its default mode, because that’s how most applications use a drive. On our first drive, polling and IOMMU passthrough would each have shaved some latency off 4K QD1 writes.

Interrupts also set a ceiling at the other end of the scale: this bench tops out near 2.8 million 4K random read IOPS, and adding fio jobs doesn’t lift it, though polling does. So on the fastest drives, our 4K random read result can sit below the spec sheet’s, and that’s our bench’s limit, not the drive’s. Our low queue depth latencies, writes especially, run higher than a tuned host would show, but they’re closer to what you’d actually see. To show the drive’s limit at both ends, the suite repeats three tests with polled I/O at the end of the random stage: the 4K random read peak, plus 4K random reads and writes at QD1. Those results get their own charts and never mix into the main ones.

4K random read and write at QD256; 128K and 1MB sequential read and write at QD64

The headline numbers, measured on a preconditioned drive instead of fresh out of the box

4K and 8K, QD1 to QD4096, eight read/write mixes from 100% read to 100% write

Servers rarely run flat out; QD1 is what latency-bound software feels, and 8K is a common database page size

4K random read at QD1024 across eight jobs, plus 4K random read and write at QD1, all with polled I/O

What the drive can do with the host’s interrupt overhead out of the way; the results to set against a spec sheet

128K and 1MB sequential reads and writes, QD1 to QD1024

How much parallelism a drive needs to reach full speed; low queue depths are what a single restore or scan gets

Random reads and writes from 512 bytes to 1MB at QD32

Writes smaller than a drive’s mapping unit can pay a read-modify-write penalty; large blocks show its bandwidth cap

4K and 8K reads and writes at QD1, QD4, and QD16, from the median (P50) to the 99.999th percentile (P99.999)

Averages hide the stalls applications notice; at a million IOPS, the slowest 0.001% is still ten requests a second

4K 70/30 at 13 queue depths from QD1 to QD4096, plotted as a share of the drive’s own peak

Finds the load where latency starts to climb

Whether sustained writes hold a flat line or sawtooth as garbage collection struggles

4K QD1 reads for four minutes right after a heavy write burst

How far reads drop after heavy writes, and how fast they recover

Write bursts after idle gaps of 0 to 300 seconds

How much write speed a quiet spell buys back

4K QD1 log writes with a sync after each, a random 8K 70/30 mix at QD16, and a 256K sequential read scan

Log-write latency, page I/O, and analytics scans, without benchmarking a database’s RAM cache

Checkpoint-sized saves and restores modeled on 8B- and 70B-class models (105GiB over eight writers, 912GiB over 64)

Time until the slowest writer finishes, which is when a real checkpoint would be done

A fixed 4K read load, alone and during a checkpoint save

What a checkpoint does to serving traffic on the same drive

Drive temperature through the hour-long sustained write test

Measured against the drive’s own warning and critical thresholds

Some things are out of scope by design. We review drives; we don’t certify them. That rules out dual-port failover, power-loss validation, and single-root I/O virtualization (SR-IOV), which belong in a qualification lab. We’ll add tests when they prove themselves on the bench. Many of the tests in the table are old standbys and still earn their place. Others are newer and require further explanation.

For one, we chart latency against load: the 70/30 4K mix from the random sweep, at 13 queue depths from QD1 to QD4096, with throughput shown as a share of the drive’s own peak. Tail latency climbs as the load grows, and the point where it turns sharply upward (on our first drive, that was write latency) represents the practical operating ceiling, or the load you can plan a server around without giving up low latency.

We also test write-to-read recovery, which measures how a drive’s reads hold up after a heavy write burst. A few minutes of 4K random writes at QD256 leave the drive with cleanup to do, and QD1 reads are then timed over the next four minutes. If a drive is still busy collecting garbage, it will read slower before climbing back; the extent and duration of the drop are the result.

Idle recovery measures what downtime buys back. After a minute of sustained writes, the drive sits idle for anywhere from zero to five minutes, then a 10-second write burst, logged second by second, shows whether background cleanup freed enough blocks to run faster.

Checkpoint interference shows what an AI checkpoint does to anything else sharing the drive. A light 4K read load, which stands in for inference or database queries, runs alone, and then again during a checkpoint save. Each read is timed from when it was due, not when it was sent, so reads stuck waiting behind a stalled one count too.

Lastly, we test thermals. Drive temperature is tracked through the hour-long sustained write test and charted against the drive's own warning and critical thresholds.

The full process means every drive is treated the same and compared fairly, with a method built to give the same results run after run. This allows us to provide a level playing field built on accurate and repeatable performance characterization.

Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

#10384. This new scorecard shows whether your favorite retailer is using Flock cameras

Automated license plate readers from Flock Safety and other vendors have become increasingly controversial across the country after reports of misuse by officers, high error rates that can lead to dangerous police encounters, and concerns about access by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.  

Flock, in particular, operates a nationwide camera network, with data from cameras operated in one jurisdiction frequently accessed by investigators from elsewhere, making it hard for local officials to understand and control privacy risks. As a result, while Flock and other providers emphasize that their cameras have been used to investigate legitimate crimes, rescue kidnapped kids, and track stolen cars, many municipalities have ended their contracts, in some cases even covering cameras awaiting removal by the service provider.   

Many businesses deploy their own automated license plate readers, or ALPRs, to track vehicles in their parking lots, sometimes sharing that information with law enforcement. But since private companies aren’t subject to freedom of information laws, it can be hard to know which businesses have them and what they’re doing with the data they collect.

To help people understand in time for the holiday shopping season which stores use the devices, Fight for the Future just released a scorecard listing 10 major retailers and what the organization knows about their use of the cameras.  

“Retailers also need to be brought into the conversation,” says Reem Suleiman, senior campaign director at Fight for the Future, which previously organized a campaign with home improvement influencers that called on Home Depot and Lowe’s to cut ties with Flock.

The chart is based on information the organization received from a questionnaire sent to the retailers and, in cases where they didn’t respond, third-party news reporting, crowdsourced camera spotting, and information from published privacy policies. “We got responses from just a handful of [businesses],” Suleiman says.  

The exact details vary, and many businesses don’t appear to use the technology at every location. Costco, for instance, told Fight for the Future that it uses ALPR cameras at “less than a dozen locations nationwide,” so it’s difficult to know just from the checklist whether your local branch of a national chain is equipped with the cameras.

But it’s easy to see at a glance that many major brands at least acknowledge in their privacy policies that they might be using the technology. Some stores also indicate that they may share information from the devices with law enforcement. 

The scorecard offers links to retailers’ emails, along with suggested text, to ask them to refrain from using ALPR technology, even if (or perhaps especially if) the details about how they do so may be opaque. Fight for the Future also encourages people to reach out with any tips about retailers that are using the cameras or with requests to add particular stores to the scoresheet. 

“We don’t have a FOIA request that we can do for companies or a public records act request that we can impose upon companies, but nothing’s stopping us from writing to them,” Suleiman says. “Nothing’s stopping people from letting these companies know what they want and what they expect.”

#10382. Gen Z is bringing back something retailers thought was dying

As consumers ready for the holiday season, it looks like gift shopping is taking a step away from the keyboard and moving back to brick-and-mortar locations.

According to research from Alchemer’s 2026 Holiday Shopper Report, more U.S. shoppers are planning to shop in physical retail stores. Some 35.8% say they will mainly shop in person, versus 31% who plan to shop mainly online.

But surprisingly, the revival of in-store shopping is being driven by a generation that mostly missed out on the mall’s heyday: Gen Z.

Research from the market research company Emarketer shows that around 51% of Gen Z are opting to shop in stores rather than online or on apps. Their preferences are showing up in spending, too. Shoppers aged 18 to 24 made 62% of their purchases in physical stores last year, compared with 52% of those 25 and older.

For Gen Z, a trip to a physical store is about more than just shopping. It’s an experience, and 63% of them say they bought something while there. The in-person shopping experience also has a social element to it. Nearly three in five Gen Z respondents say they shop as a way to spend time with others.

The clothing aisle is leading the way back to the store, as around one in five Gen Zers say they visit a clothing store every month, twice the rate of all adults.

Emarketer also found that many retailers are tapping into the renewed interest in real-world shopping, particularly catering to Gen Z. For instance, many are leaning on building community through in-store programming, like ornament making and letter-writing workshops at Macy’s, or fragrance readings at Lush, the personal care retailer.

A unifying trend across ages is a low tolerance for friction. Customers are looking for smooth shopping experiences. Alchemer’s survey found that shoppers are particularly sensitive to disruptions like slow checkouts and items being out of stock.

A São Paulo businessman has been arrested by police on suspicion of sending a game console stuffed with explosives to the electronics store of a rival in an attempt to kill him. The device then exploded. On Monday, Military Police executed a warrant against Everton Yoshizumi Lima, who is suspected of perpetrating the outrageous attack, G1 reports.

On October 23, 2026, at around 5:30 pm, a delivery person dropped off a video game console at an electronics repair shop, with the cover that it was being left for modifications requested by the customer. Police say the device had an explosive planted inside that was programmed to detonate upon receipt. "Unaware of its contents, the store owner put the video game console in a drawer and continued working," the report states. The device ignited and exploded, causing severe damage and injuring two people: the owner of the store and a friend who was at the scene. The whole thing was captured on video, which you can see by expanding the tweet below:

Empresário é preso suspeito de enviar videogame com explosivos que detonaram em loja de eletrônicos de Santo André, Grande SP https://t.co/EqXSlkM1J9 #g1 https://t.co/H3naAgNzlVNovember 16, 2026

The device was found to have two explosive charges of the same magnitude inside, but only one of the devices went off, possibly limiting the capacity for damage and injury. The report notes that investigators believe the intent of the device was to kill the victim, given the amount of explosives. The console was delivered to the store by an unsuspecting motorcyclist who was working for a delivery app company and had no idea they were carrying a bomb.

The request appears to have been traced back to Lima, who is the main suspect in the attack. Lima purportedly owns other electronics stores in the area, including two on the same street where this store was recently opened, labeling the motive as "business competition." "The new store had been advertised through a social media campaign and the distribution of flyers," the report states. "Annoyed by the competition, the suspect allegedly decided to eliminate the competitor, according to the line of investigation."

According to the report, Lima was arrested during the course of an investigation into a possible motorcycle theft. It appears that Lima was the owner of the target vehicle, and that police visited in advance, suspecting someone might try to steal it. While checking his data, it was found that Lima had an outstanding arrest warrant for his suspected involvement in the attack.

#10379. Target earnings: Retailer reports strong sales momentum ahead of the holidays as TGT stock soars in 2026

Retail giant Target Corporation (NYSE: TGT) has reported its third-quarter earnings for fiscal 2026, and they are a night-and-day difference compared to the results posted for the same quarter a year earlier.

Target’s sales growth for the period was the best in half a decade, suggesting that a turnaround plan from its new CEO is working. Here’s what you need to know.

Target’s Q3 2026 at a glance

This morning before the opening bell, Target reported its Q3 2026 earnings, a period that ended on October 31. By and large, the results were music to investors’ ears:

  • Net sales: $27.1 billion (up 7.1% YOY)
  • Adjusted earnings per share (EPS): $2.65 (up 74.8%)
  • Operating income: $1.67 billion (up 76.4%)
  • Net earnings: $1.21 billion (up 75.8%)

It should be noted that Target’s Q3 was helped somewhat by tariff refunds. During the quarter, the company received $301 million back through refunds.

Those refunds contributed $228 million to net earnings as well as 50 cents to the company’s earnings per share for the quarter.

Even so, Target handily beat analyst expectations on several fronts, notes CNBC. Analysts had expected revenue of $26.5 billion and an EPS of $2.07. Even after discounting the 50 cent EPS tariff boost, Target would still have topped analysts’ expectations on earnings per share by 8 cents.

Announcing the results, Target’s CEO, Michael Fiddelke, who took the helm in February and immediately launched a turnaround effort, said the company’s “third-quarter results reflect continued progress against our strategic priorities, centered on serving busy families with our signature blend of style, design and value.”

Target’s turnaround efforts appear to be working

A year ago, Target’s business looked much bleaker than it does today. The company was facing challenges on multiple fronts.

Many retailers at that time were also facing some of those same challenges: increased tariffs and customers cutting back on discretionary spending as inflationary pressure bit into their pocketbooks.

But Target was also facing a set of challenges unique to itself. Declining foot traffic had been driven by self-inflicted wounds over the years, including understaffed stores, messier merchandising, and DEI rollbacks that prompted a significant boycott of the company.

When Fiddelke took the reins in February, he sought to correct many of these issues, implementing sweeping changes, including a refined merchandising strategy that complemented Target’s strengths relative to competitors (such as well-designed home and apparel offerings). 

He also began remodeling stores to give them a new, modern look, and increased staffing at those stores to better meet customers’ needs.

Those changes appear to be working. Target says that in Q3, comparable foot traffic grew by 5%, while net sales grew 7.1% compared to last year. As CNBC noted, that’s Target’s best sales growth in more than five years.

TGT shares have soared in 2026

A strong Q3 has led Target to update its expectations for fiscal year 2026.

The company is now in its all-important Q4, which covers the end-of-year holiday period. For fiscal 2026, Target says it now expects full-year net sales growth in a range of around 6%, which is one point higher than the 5% the company initially forecast.

Still, despite the strong Q3 results, TGT shares are currently down about 1.1% in premarket trading, as of this writing.

Some of that may be attributed to profit-taking. Target’s stock price has surged by more than 60% this year, and investors often decide to lock in profits after a good quarter.

However, the drop in the company’s stock price may also signal investor concern about Target’s future business. There’s no doubt that Target was helped this quarter by its tariff refunds. But those refunds won’t keep coming forever.

Additionally, Target said it expects its capex to be between $5 billion and $6 billion in 2027. That is an increase of $1 billion from what Target spent in 2026.

While such spending may benefit Target in the long term, it can impact near-term growth, and investors generally think in the near term.

#10377. An Eric Trump-backed startup unveils a powerful new humanoid robot—and won’t rule out arming it

Foundation Future Industries, a startup backed by Eric Trump, has unveiled a humanoid robot that can carry 200 pounds while walking through rain, snow, and dust. The company wants its new Phantom MKII to work on construction sites and in factories—but the CEO isn’t ruling out putting weapons in its hands.

Sankaet Pathak, founder and CEO of Foundation, tells Fast Company his company would consider arming its machines if asked to by the U.S. military, arguing that deploying robots on the ground could reduce reliance on drones and air strikes.

“We’re not anti-weaponization and warfare,” he says. “That’s not something we have a blanket policy of just saying we’re not going to do.”

Phantom MKII is a second-generation humanoid designed for heavy industry and defense, unveiled today alongside Cortex II, the AI system that controls it. Foundation, which counts Eric Trump among its investors and advisers, has been particularly open about military applications—at times drawing controversy.

Earlier this month, the Financial Times reported that Foundation’s cofounder and president, Mike LeBlanc, was in direct talks with the Israel Defense Forces to supply up to 1,000 of its first-generation Phantom MKI robots for operations in tunnels beneath Gaza. Pathak disputes that characterization. “We’re not in talks with the IDF in any official capacity on deploying robots there,” he says. “What we have are very early exploration conversations.” When pressed about LeBlanc’s comments, Pathak says there is “literally nothing actively going on,” and there are no conversations progressing toward a contract.

Previously, Foundation said its machines had been tested with Ukrainian forces, while LeBlanc has described potential uses for them in detecting booby traps and trip wires.

For now, Pathak says most of Foundation’s defense work focuses on logistics rather than combat—though he doesn’t rule out deploying his machines on the battlefield. “Any time DOW [Department of War] will come to us and say, ‘Well, we need these robots more on the active battlefield with a weapon,’ to me that indicates that means less drones, less air strikes, more precision,” he says.

Pathak believes ground-based robots could accomplish military objectives without bombing entire buildings, potentially shortening wars.

Whether deployed in war or on construction sites, which Pathak sees as the robot’s ideal initial use, the Phantom MKII is designed to be more capable than its predecessor. Foundation says the robot has weather-resistant joints and modular parts that can be replaced in the field, along with a battery that can run for up to six hours, though heavier payloads reduce that figure. At maximum capacity, Pathak says the machine can walk while carrying 200 pounds, compared with roughly 50 to 60 pounds for the previous version.

The Phantom MKII can do so thanks to significant redesigns of its actuators, the motors and gearing that make its limbs move. Its joints have been shrunk to around three-quarters the size of its predecessor’s, Pathak says, while delivering more than 1.5 times the performance. Smaller also means somewhat cheaper. Pathak claims the company has halved its bill of materials cost while simplifying assembly to make large-scale manufacturing more practical.

The goal is to begin producing MKII robots in early 2027. Initially, the company hopes to manufacture several hundred before ramping up to a few thousand by the end of the year. Production will initially remain in the San Francisco Bay Area; Pathak claims most components now come from the U.S. or allied countries.

Alongside the hardware improvements, Foundation claims a significant leap forward in the software powering the machine. Its Cortex II artificial intelligence system is designed to learn physical tasks by observing humans perform them—requiring as few as 60 demonstrations for some tasks.

Pathak’s ambitions extend beyond construction sites and battlefields, though he rules out selling to countries that aren’t allied with the United States. In a manifesto published alongside the robot’s launch, Pathak outlines a vision of the future in which fleets of robots work in mining, materials processing, and construction. Humanoids could help bring the cost of a $1 million home down to between $60,000 and $80,000, he figures.

Beyond building your next home, the Phantom MKII could help keep it safe, too. Pathak is open to his robots taking on policing roles, provided they are deployed in ways that make people feel protected rather than intimidated. “I don’t think you can build a utopia and then not defend it,” he says.

#10376. It’s launch day for ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’. The 13-year wait is over at midnight

After a 13-year wait, one of entertainment’s biggest releases is finally here.

“Grand Theft Auto VI” launches Thursday, sending players back to Vice City and testing whether Rockstar Games can follow one of the bestselling video games ever made with another cultural and commercial phenomenon.

The latest installment becomes playable at midnight local time on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X’S, meaning players in Asia and other regions will begin entering the game hours before its U.S. release.

New Zealand will be among the first countries where players can access the game and internet providers there are preparing for a surge in downloads as midnight arrives.

“The game file size at 212 gigabytes is unprecedented,” said Kurt Rodgers, network strategy manager for Chorus New Zealand. “That’s more than a quarter of the average household’s data usage in an entire month, all in one go.”

The company expects about 35 petabytes of additional traffic across its network, which Rodgers called “enormous.”

The expectations are enormous, too.

The “Grand Theft Auto” franchise has sold more than 470 million units worldwide, while “Grand Theft Auto V,” released in 2013, accounts for more than 230 million of those sales and reached $1 billion in retail sales in just three days.

Rockstar is returning to Vice City, its fictionalized version of Miami, with two new protagonists, a sprawling Florida-inspired world and the pressure of following a game that became one of the most successful entertainment products ever released.

Game returns to Vice City after 13 years

At the center of “GTA VI” are Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple whose attempts to improve their lives pull them deeper into the criminal underworld of Leonida, Rockstar’s fictionalized version of Florida.

Lucia has recently been released from prison, while Jason is a former soldier who became involved with drug runners in the Leonida Keys. When a criminal job goes wrong, the pair become entangled in a wider conspiracy.

Their relationship marks one of the biggest departures from “Grand Theft Auto V,” which followed three playable protagonists.

Rockstar has promoted Leonida as its largest and most detailed open world yet, stretching beyond Vice City into beaches, highways, wetlands, nightlife districts and smaller communities inspired by South Florida.

Developers immersed themselves in the region while building the game, driving through Miami, the Florida Keys and surrounding communities. They flew over the Everglades and researched the area’s history and architecture.

Miami embraces its fictional alter ego

Miami and surrounding communities have leaned into their connection to Vice City ahead of the release, with businesses, sports teams and local governments using the game’s arrival as a marketing opportunity.

Miami-Dade County entered into a $3.9 million promotional deal with Rockstar that includes a giant “Welcome to Vice City” display atop the Miami Heat’s Kaseya Center. The NBA team is also scheduled to wear black-and-pink Vice City uniforms on the eve of the game’s release.

The campaign has not been universally welcomed. Some South Florida officials have questioned whether public resources should be used to promote a franchise known for car theft, gunplay and other criminal activity.

Supporters have argued that the enormous attention surrounding “GTA VI” gives the region an opportunity to capitalize on a global spotlight.

In Seoul, a giant advertisement draped the side of a building, while Warner Music will host a party at a bar Thursday themed around the game’s soundtrack.

Years of hype arrive at launch day

Few entertainment releases arrive with this much anticipation.

The first “GTA VI” trailer drew more than 93 million YouTube views in its first 24 hours, while Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar’s parent company, has said the second trailer generated more than 475 million views across platforms in a day.

The game also has attracted awards attention before most players have had a chance to explore it.

“GTA VI” received eight nominations Tuesday for the Game Awards, including game of the year, game direction, narrative, art direction, score and music, audio design, action/adventure and performance. The awards will be presented Dec. 10.

The long wait is partly a product of the extraordinary staying power of its predecessor. “Grand Theft Auto Online,” the multiplayer component of “GTA V,” has kept players engaged for years through updates, activities and in-game purchases.

Music has long been woven into the “Grand Theft Auto” experience, with fictional radio stations and carefully curated soundtracks accompanying players as they drive through the series’ cities.

For “GTA VI,” Rockstar commissioned an original adaptive score from Grammy-winning French electronic duo Justice. The music is designed to shift depending on where players are and what they are doing. A 30-track “Grand Theft Auto VI: Original Score” is scheduled for release Dec. 11 and includes collaborations involving Tame Impala, SZA, King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard and Gesaffelstein.

What players will find next

Despite years of trailers and promotional material, Rockstar has kept significant portions of “GTA VI” under wraps.

The full voice cast has not been revealed, including the performers behind Lucia and Jason. Actor Stephen Root has confirmed to The Associated Press that he appears in the game, though Rockstar has not publicly identified his role.

Questions also remain about the full range of characters, locations, activities and gameplay systems waiting inside Leonida.

Those answers will begin emerging first from players in Asia and Europe as midnight arrives in their regions, followed by North America hours later.

Associated Press journalists Charlotte Graham-McLay and Tong-hyung Kim contributed to this report.

—Jonathan Landrum Jr., AP Entertainment Writer

#10374. 5 Best AI Anime Video Generators in 2026, and Are AI Anime Videos Worth Making?

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI video generators can now turn a prompt or a character image into a few seconds of animation, and anime is one of the most popular styles people ask for. But anime is also one of the hardest styles to get right: flat colors, thin linework and stylized motion expose the weaknesses of video models quickly. For developers and designers, the useful question is not which tool is “best”, but what each one actually offers, what it cannot do yet, and how to fit it into a real production workflow.

This article compares five generators on what their own pages state, covers the problems they all share, asks whether AI anime videos are worth making, and then explains how the models work and how designers and developers can build a practical workflow, including ffmpeg and API-integration examples. “Best” here depends on the job: the tools are listed in no ranking order, each is linked once to its official site for reference, and the comparison is based on public vendor pages reviewed in November 2026. Features, models and pricing change often, so verify current details before relying on any of them.

We reviewed each vendor’s own site and compared what it states on the same points. This is a documentation-based comparison, not a lab benchmark. Where a page does not state something, we say so instead of guessing.

AI anime video generator by Pollo AI sits within a general AI video platform. On its main site, Pollo describes generating video from text prompts or uploaded images and editing existing videos, such as adding, changing, removing or restyling content. It also offers AI image generation, so a character image and the animation can be made in one place.

Strengths for anime work: text-to-video and image-to-video in the same tool, plus video editing and restyling, which suits experimenting with looks.

Limitations and gaps: the pages we could read do not name the underlying models, list credit amounts or pricing, or describe anime-specific controls such as reference characters or first and last frame inputs. You will need to test consistency yourself.

Fits: creators who want image, video and editing tools in one platform and are comfortable testing results before committing.

Vidu lists text-to-video, image-to-video and reference-to-video modes. For image-to-video you can set first and last frames. Reference-to-video lets you upload several images of a character, object or scene, and saved references can be reused through a My References feature. The site highlights 2D animation and diverse artistic styles, mentions 1080p output and offers an API platform aimed at enterprise use.

Strengths for anime work: the clearest set of consistency tools among the five pages we reviewed, with first and last frames, multi-image references and reusable saved characters.

Limitations and gaps: the page does not specify clip durations beyond examples, detail its anime-specific templates, or list prices. Free credits are mentioned without an amount.

Fits: sequences built around a recurring character, and teams that want an API.

Kling AI presents Kling 4.0 for video, described as offering stable dynamic motion and an audio-visual experience, alongside an image model, a Motion Control tool and a node-based Canvas editor for working through scripts, storyboards, images and video. It also lists MCP and CLI support for batch generation and automated production, and an API platform with documentation.

Strengths for anime work: motion-focused tooling and a workflow environment for storyboards and multi-step production, plus automation options for developers.

Limitations and gaps: the page we reviewed does not detail image-to-video specifics, first and last frame controls, camera control, durations, video resolution or pricing, and it gives no anime-specific guidance.

Fits: teams that value motion control and scripted or batch pipelines.

Hailuo AI, from MiniMax, describes creating AI videos and images from text or photos. Its page shows a reference field and an Omni Reference option, a banner for a model that mentions multimodal generation and editing, and many photo-based templates such as photo-to-motion, transformation and style transfer.

Strengths for anime work: an accessible, template-driven way to animate a still image and try stylized effects quickly.

Limitations and gaps: the page does not explain how reference works, or state camera control, durations, resolution, API availability or pricing. Template-driven results may be harder to control precisely than prompt- and frame-driven workflows.

Fits: quick experiments and social clips made from a single image.

Dreamina describes itself as an all-in-one creative platform for images, videos and talking avatars. For video it lists text-to-video, image-to-video, sketch-to-video, cartoon video generation and reference-to-video, using several Seedance models, along with editing examples such as green-screen replacement. It also offers image generation and upscaling.

Strengths for anime work: a broad toolset, including cartoon-oriented generation, references and editing in one environment.

Limitations and gaps: no official maximum duration or video resolution is stated, and the page notes that displayed pricing is for reference only and that final pricing requires signing in. The breadth of features and models can make it harder to know which one to use for a given shot.

Fits: creators who want images, video and avatars under one roof.

“Not stated” means the vendor page we reviewed did not say, not that the feature does not exist. Treat the table as a checklist of questions to answer in your own tests.

It depends on the job and on what you compare them with. Against a full studio production they are limited. Against having no animation at all, they change what a small team or solo creator can attempt.

Treat the generator as a fast prototyping and shot-making assistant, not a replacement for writing, direction and design. Audience reaction also varies, and some viewers are openly critical of AI-made work, so quality and disclosure both matter.

Most current generators are diffusion models extended to video. As in image diffusion, the model starts from random noise and removes it step by step, guided by your inputs. The extension to video, described in research such as Video Diffusion Models, is that the model denoises a whole sequence of frames together, so that motion and appearance stay coherent over time. Many systems work in a compressed latent space rather than on raw pixels to keep generation affordable.

Create an original character sheet with front, side and three-quarter views, a fixed color palette and a clear silhouette. Keep it simple: fewer fine details means less flicker.

Break the sequence into short shots with one action and one camera move each. A four-shot, twenty-second sequence is more realistic than one long generation.

Start each shot from a clean keyframe of your character. Where a tool supports first and last frames or reference images, use them to define the pose and keep identity stable.

Describe subject, action, camera and mood, and add a style anchor. For example: “The girl slowly turns toward the camera, wind moves her hair, petals drift past, gentle push-in, 2D cel shading, clean linework.”

Scrub through each clip for warped hands, drifting faces and flickering lines. Discard or regenerate failures instead of hoping nobody notices.

Join the best takes, color-match them, add sound and captions, and add disclosure where a platform requires it.

Developers can make the pipeline repeatable. Two patterns help: scripted post-processing with ffmpeg, and a resilient job-based client for any generation API.

The script below extracts a last frame to seed the next shot, normalizes clips to a common size and frame rate so they can be joined, concatenates them, and optionally holds each frame twice for an “on twos” look. Adjust sizes and frame rates to your project.

Video generation is usually asynchronous: you submit a job, then poll or receive a callback. The sketch below shows the pattern with a timeout and backoff. The endpoints and fields are placeholders, so follow your provider’s documentation for real ones.

Most are diffusion models for video. They start from noise and remove it step by step across a sequence of frames, guided by a text prompt and often a starting image or reference images, until coherent motion appears.

Usually, for consistency. The image locks the character and style, while the prompt only needs to describe motion.

Thin lines and flat color regions make small frame-to-frame changes visible. Simpler designs, slower motion and post-processing reduce it.

Partly. Reference images, saved characters and shared keyframes help, but you should still review every shot for drift.

For short clips, concept previews and storyboards, often yes. For long, dialogue-driven stories, not yet.

It depends on the tool and plan. Read the current terms and make sure you have rights to any characters or assets you upload.

Run the same character image and prompt through each, then compare consistency, line stability, motion quality and cost per usable second.

AI anime video generators are useful, but uneven. The five tools reviewed here differ in input modes, consistency tools, developer access and how much their own pages say, and none removes the core problems of consistency, flicker and limited acting. The practical approach is to test several tools on the same shots, keep your workflow tool-agnostic, design characters that are simple and consistent, and review every clip before it ships. Used that way, they are a capable prototyping and shot-making aid, not a substitute for design and direction.

Phison’s Pascari X201P meets its rated specs and pairs 12 GB/s sequential writes with a steady 600K random write IOPS, making short work of AI checkpoints. It gives ground at low and moderate queue depths, where QD1 writes and mixed workloads lag, and it ran warm on our bench.

Mixed-workload performance trails at middle QDs

Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Phison is serious about enterprise storage, and the Pascari X201P was not released lightly; it came in the night, under NDA, alongside this week’s Supercomputing 2026 event. The drive is part of the Performance X-Series, which handles intensive workloads where consistency is the name of the game. We were nevertheless pleasantly surprised by its write performance, with a steady 12 GB/s for sequential and over 600,000 random write IOPS, considering it’s marketed at the 1 drive write per day (DWPD) endurance point.

Part of that surprise comes from the fact that this is Phison’s read-intensive PCIe 5.0 data center drive, a successor to the X200P. It comes in the U.2 form factor — which can be more convenient in many cases — from 1.92TB to 30.72TB, and an E3.S version from 3.84TB, in both single- and dual-port models. It stands next to its mixed-use sibling, the X201E, which is the one rated for 3 DWPD. What makes the X201P exciting, in part, is its own 16-channel X2 controller and the flash that’s inside.

This drive is aimed at AI, analytics, and database servers, with its case made in the 4K 70/30 mix at higher queue depths. It passed Phison’s one-million-IOPS mark at QD128 in our testing of the 15.36TB model, and the drive met all of its rated specs, though its random read rating required polled I/O to reach on our bench. It faced challenges with QD1 writes, log commits, and the middle range of our mixed sweeps. Given its blend of performance, capacity, and endurance, we consider it a very competent entry from the company that was perhaps better known in the consumer SSD market until recently.

The drive met or beat every rated performance figure that we can test, which should be the target of any enterprise SSD released today. If there’s an exception, it’s due to how we test; Phison lists a ceiling of 3,250K IOPS for 4K random read, which is higher than our bench allows with our interrupt-driven I/O, which we use rather than a polled approach. We also run a polled test on every drive for cases like this, and our result was 3,283K IOPS at the same queue depth Phison specifies, which shows the drive does exceed its specification.

Datacenter NVMe SSD v2.0, with v2.6 telemetry features

PCIe 5.0 x4, single port (2x2 dual-port models offered)

ISE, SED (TCG Opal 2.02) or non-SED; AES-XTS 256-bit

512-byte and 4,096-byte, each with optional metadata

Six: 25 W, 22 W, 20 W, 18 W, 15 W and 12 W maximum

Host-controlled thermal management supported

Our sample is in the U.2 form factor, 15mm thick. We have the single-port SKU, ISE model XP208H0815T3P3216T310, with firmware X2WM6026. Some data we previously saw from the drive was reportedly on X2WM6025, but we confirmed X2WM6026 for all relevant results. We mounted the drive on a PCIe 5.0 x4 add-in card adapter for U.2, standing upright in the slot.

Phison did not provide firm hardware details, but we were able to discover some things on our own. The flash was probably the easiest, as the company claimed it was a 321-layer part. That can only be SK hynix’s V9 TLC, which is not flash we’ve tested before in any product. It’s exceptionally fast and uses a three-deck design, which is relatively new for TLC flash. The flash could be credited with some of the exceptional performance measurements we see on the drive.

As for the proprietary controller, we’ve heard that it’s using a combination of the standard Arm Cortex-R5 — these would be the main cores — with AndesCore RISC-V on the side. We’ve seen the latter before on the Phison E28 consumer SSD controller, which did have some enterprise-like aspects to it. The E28 is the newer design, built on a 6nm process with Andes’ newer N45 cores alongside the N25F, while the X2 is a 12nm part that, as far as we can tell, sticks with N25F-class co-processors.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

In this case, the X2 has twice the flash channels, which enables a superior level of performance out of TLC flash, as in enterprise you do not rely on pSLC. That mix of cores sets the X2 apart from other 16-channel PCIe 5.0 enterprise controllers: Marvell’s Bravera SC5 and Silicon Motion’s SM8366 rely on Arm cores throughout, whereas Phison pairs its Cortex-R5 cores with small RISC-V co-processors.

#10371. How a tiny Italian soccer team plans to beat the biggest clubs in Europe

Como 1907 is a tiny European soccer team. It plays in a town of 85,000 people on Lake Como in northern Italy, where some Hollywood royalty live for part of the year. Its stadium holds only 12,000, which makes it a school playground next to Real Madrid’s 83,000-capacity Santiago Bernabéu. The owners of Como, Indonesia’s billionaire Hartono family, aim to beat Real Madrid, along with the likes of Paris Saint-Germain, Arsenal, and Bayern Munich.

Not on the pitch, necessarily, even though this year Como made it for the first time to the UEFA Champions League, the top club competition in Europe and the world. Its president, Mirwan Suwarso, wants to turn the little team into a financial powerhouse. Since Como will never match the TV and ticket money of Europe’s giants, he is trying to outgrow them as a brand. He wants Como to play in Disney’s league, not only the Champions League.

Suwarso sees soccer as the attraction. “There is a merchandise arm, the same as Disney,” he told The Observer in October. “The stadium, coming to a game, is the theme park. It is where you can touch and feel it, where you can experience the magic of Como.”

He expects nonsoccer revenue to overtake soccer revenue within two or three years, and already values the club at $1.1 billion. Como already has a fashion and hospitality business. You may have seen A-listers in its stands on Instagram. It sells match-day hospitality in rented lakeside villas, and its sister companies run a travel agency, a property arm, a youth academy, and a digital-content unit. Eventually, the club will offer more than that, as the brand’s presence expands across the world.

Como’s latest money-making move is kits. Adidas, current maker of its game jerseys and shorts, pays no sponsorship fee to Como, unlike some of the top teams in the world. European teams like Real Madrid get about $139 million a year on average. In addition to that, Real Madrid gets a 22.5% cut on anything with its brand sold through Adidas channels once sales pass a set threshold, along with bonuses for winning major titles like the Champions League or the Spanish league, La Liga. Como, like most teams, gets none of that.

Instead, Como and its small team brethren get gear for their teams. For Como, that’s $300,000 to $400,000 worth of it, which probably costs $100,000 to make, says Suwarso. He points out that they need to buy millions of dollars in kits from Adidas to sell to fans. From those sales they get a cut. Suwarso thinks this type of deal is upside down for small clubs. Adidas declined to comment for this story.

Suwarso’s answer is to own the whole chain, from the shirt’s design to the shop shelf. And they want to share this design, manufacturing, and distribution business with other small clubs so they all can get more money.

Como’s Adidas deal ends after the 2026-27 season. The club won’t renew it, and it plans to launch its own kit brand in June. Suwarso doesn’t pretend Como will make Real Madrid money this way. Real Madrid will make more because “of course, they’re bigger,” he said.

Peter Rohlmann, a German sports-marketing consultant who runs PR Marketing, a firm in Rheine, thinks Como is overreaching. In-house jerseys have failed within a few years in the vast majority of cases, even at big clubs, he says. Fans resist little-known labels, clubs underestimate the costs, and production never reaches real volume, he points out in an email interview. Napoli, another Italian soccer club, is the only one that survived with its Armani-designed kits. “All others have failed,” Rohlmann told the Sports Business Journal back in August.

Lecce, another team that plays in Italy’s Serie A league, tried to launch its own homemade brand, M908, starting in 2018. M908’s sales were only around $2.3 million a year, according to News Tank Football. This July, the club announced that Adidas would take over starting with the 2026-27 season.

Como’s management believes they can fix this volume problem by selling to other clubs. The club will join forces with “a historic Italian label”—Como hasn’t identified it yet—to make its new kit brand, according to FashionNetwork, while it dresses clubs across Europe and South America. Its Rhude 4 Fans line, launched in April 2026, already makes collections for Tottenham Hotspur and Everton in England’s Premier League, and Los Angeles FC, in Major League Soccer. The Observer counts 24 clubs that Como helps with merchandise. The kits are for “fellow unwanteds and undesirables,” says Suwarso. The teams that Nike, Adidas, and Puma won’t pay.

Como will carry the bill, says Alexandra Bell, the club’s chief communications officer. “We will underwrite production, marketing, and distribution costs, making it a no-risk proposition for partner clubs,” she tells Fast Company in an email. The kit’s design will be the product of “a collaboration between our creative team and our partner’s designers,” she says.

Bell tells me that only Como’s players will wear the new kits next season, as the company fine-tunes the manufacturing. “On the lifestyle side, this newly formed brand have already reached agreements to support nine other clubs next season, and that number continues to grow,” she says.

Como has its work cut out for it, as brands like Skechers, On (which got the French star Kylian Mbappé to promote its gear), New Balance, and Under Armour all try to gain a foothold in European soccer. Still, Bell is confident, given Como’s background in design and production.

“Just like any business, risk cannot be eliminated,” she tells me, but the club’s retail team already handles everything “from design, production and supply chain to logistics, distribution and e-commerce,” including six shops in Como itself and 585 affiliate shops across the province. In four years, she says, that operation grew from about $59,000 a year to a business that’s targeting about $44 million in annual revenue in 2026.

Perhaps Como will succeed where others failed. The club has a special allure, a je ne sais quoi that makes it very attractive to people. Part of it lies in its David-versus-Goliath story. The Hartonos helped the club mount a formidable comeback, taking the team back to Italy’s top division. (The club had been as low as the fourth tier of the Italian game at one point.) They surprised everyone last year, when Como finished fourth in Serie A. This got the club into the 2026-2027 Champions League, where it is near the top of the standings as of November. 

Another part of the club’s attraction is the high-class setting of Lake Como and all the glamour the stars who vacation there bring to the public’s collective imagination. Hugh Grant, Keira Knightley, Michael Fassbender, and Florence Pugh have all turned up at the Stadio Sinigaglia at one point. Many came while vacationing on the lake. The French soccer icon Thierry Henry and Como’s coach, Cesc Fàbregas—a FIFA World Cup winner with Spain—own stakes in the club. According to Goal, a former employee told La Gazzetta dello Sport, Italy’s leading sports daily, that the club treats famous guests to all-inclusive weekends. This helps Como position itself as an aspirational brand. 

Selling the experience

The Hartono brothers, Robert Budi and Michael, bought Como in 2019. Back then, the team was stuck in Italy’s fourth division, playing semi-professional soccer. It seemed like a losing team, but the brothers saw opportunity: a potentially huge business that could go well beyond the sport. Fashion, travel, hospitality, all built around the club and the picture-perfect Lake Como brand. 

The Hartonos set up Sent Retail, a sister company that shares a holding with a property arm and a travel agency. According to Gazzetta, the company is separate from the club. It also has its own retail and fashion arm. Called Curva, it sells its own label alongside other clubs’ merchandise. AC Milan gear is its best seller, Suwarso says. Curva also stocks Venezia, Bologna, and AS Roma gear, and more clubs are coming, Bell tells me.

“Our vision is for Curva to become a multibrand fashion destination inspired by football culture—think Kith for football culture,” she says, referring to the New York streetwear store.

They got Rhuigi Villaseñor—founder of the Los Angeles label Rhude and a Como shareholder—as its chief brand officer. He has been busy ever since. Villaseñor’s streetwear label Rhude worked with Adidas to drop limited-edition fourth kits. The club also worked with the Indonesian couture designer Didit Hediprasetyo to create the club’s main home and away jerseys, incorporating Lake Como water and marble patterns painted by the Switzerland-based artist Golnaz Jebelli.

The company got the Italian luxury menswear house Brioni to design the suits for the squad and the Milanese luggage maker Bric to make cobranded leather duffel bags and travel accessories. Hublot, the Swiss watchmaker, created a 50-piece limited-edition Classic Fusion black ceramic chronograph featuring the club crest.

The company also produces its own resortwear and leisure apparel via the Official Como 1907 Store under fictional country club labels like Como Sailing Club, Como Running Club, and Como Padel Club. There are Lago di Como lines for running, tennis, padel, and the outdoors. To give you an idea of price, they sell a quilted leather bomber for about $1,740.

Is it working?

That postcard travels well in every sense of the word. Only 38% of its merchandise is soccer gear, according to the Sunday Times. More than 40% of lifestyle sales come from the United States, versus around 17% from Italy, Suwarso said at the Pambianco-PwC Fashion Summit in Milan on November 11, according to FashionNetwork. Como is hunting for a flagship store in London, and Paris and Milan are next, Bell says.

According to Suwarso, more than 80% of the group’s nearly 300 employees don’t work in the club itself at all. The club, however, is still the key to it all. Its social following grew 202% in a year, to nearly 4 million. Stadium revenue nearly tripled in a year, from about $5.5 million to $15.5 million. Almost all of that jump came from hospitality, Suwarso told Business of Sport. While Como fans pay $23 for basic tickets, top hospitality packages reach about $2,900. “With a 12,000-seat stadium, there are limits to how much we can grow through match day revenue alone,” Bell says.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Destination Calcio (@destination.calcio)

For all of Suwarso’s optimism, Rohlmann sees a new Borussia Dortmund. The German club went public on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange in 2000, and Rohlmann says Como, like Dortmund back then, is trying things “out of euphoria and because of the need for storytelling.” Dortmund spent its IPO money on an expensive squad and a bigger stadium, sold the stadium and leased it back, and by 2005 was hours away from bankruptcy, with debts of around $140 million.

So far, however, the numbers seem to be on Suwarso’s side.

These aren’t audited figures but, in addition to the $44 million in annual retail revenue this year, the club itself claims its revenue also jumped from $11.4 million in the 2023-24 season to $64.3 million in 2024-25. But so did the losses: $122 million for the club itself in 2024-25 and $153 million for the whole group, according to Gazzetta.

Costs nearly tripled that season, to $184 million, with staff costs alone at $99 million, according to Calcio e Finanza, an Italian sports finance site. The Hartonos have put in about $450 million, much of it on players: Como has spent about $470 million on transfers since the 2023-24 season, according to Outside Sports, a sports business site. In June, Gazzetta predicted that Como would “inevitably exceed” the financial rules of UEFA, the European federation. These rules ban clubs from spending too much money beyond a certain level of financial loss. 

These rules are designed to avoid billionaires from using their resources to win competitions, even if their teams are losing money, thus making other clubs with no financial backup less competitive. “If you have to fine us, fine us,” Suwarso told Business of Sport. The club is expected to agree a settlement with UEFA around April or May 2027, according to Outside Sports.

Suwarso promises that the club will break even by the end of next season. “Our priority is a sustainable club,” Bell says. “Performance on the pitch is unpredictable, and commercial growth does not automatically translate into results.”

We will see soon enough. If Suwarso is right, Como will continue making more money selling its brand than playing with its crest. If Rohlmann is right, they will end up with the most expensive gift shop south of the Alps.

#10369. Top 6 AI Text to Speech Tools in 2026: Features, Strengths and Limits

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Not long ago, a synthetic voice was easy to spot: flat, rushed and strangely stressed. Today, the best AI text to speech tools can read a script with natural pacing, switch accents, whisper or laugh on cue, and even speak in a voice cloned from a short recording. That makes them useful far beyond screen readers. Developers use them for product voice prompts, marketers for video voiceovers, teachers for course narration and writers for listening back to their own drafts.

This guide explains how modern text-to-speech works, what to look for when choosing a tool, and compares six options: OpenArt, ElevenLabs, Murf AI, Speechify, WellSaid Labs and Amazon Polly. Each section covers strengths, limits and the best use case. The details come from each vendor’s own pages at the time of writing, and plans, models and prices change often, so confirm current terms before you commit.

OpenArt’s AI text to speech tool lives inside a wider creative platform. You open the Audio tab, choose Create voice-over, select a model, paste your script, pick a voice, generate, listen and download. It runs in the browser with nothing to install. According to OpenArt’s page, you can switch between models for each script, including Fish Audio Drama 3, Eleven v4 and Eleven v4 Turbo.

The direction system is what makes it practical for storytelling. You add notes in square brackets, such as [whispering], [laughs] or [pause], directly in the script. OpenArt says Fish Audio Drama 3 gives close control over single words and mid-line changes of mood, while Eleven v4 reads the whole script to infer the emotion of each line and keeps the voice steady when you regenerate a line. Preset voices are labeled by accent, gender and age, and you can upload a recording of your own voice to clone it.

Because OpenArt also makes video and background music, you can build the voiceover, visuals and soundtrack in one place. It describes a Director mode for planning stories up to five minutes, and the voiceover can also be added in any video editor.

Pricing: New accounts get 40 free credits. Paid plans add monthly credits and watermark-free downloads, and commercial rights apply on eligible paid plans. Check the pricing page for current plans.

Best for: creators who want expressive voiceovers together with AI video and music.

ElevenLabs is one of the best-known names in AI voice. Its text to speech page describes a large voice library, voice design and both instant and professional voice cloning, with the latest model, Eleven v4, positioned as the most expressive. It also lists Eleven v3, Multilingual v2 and a low-latency Flash and Turbo family aimed at real-time use, and it claims support for more than 90 languages and accents, with the exact count varying by model.

For developers, there is a text to speech API with SDKs, which makes it practical for apps, games, agents and automated pipelines. The free plan includes 10,000 credits a month, and paid plans start with Starter at $6 a month, then Creator at $22 and Pro at $99, according to the vendor page, with introductory offers on the first month.

Pricing: Free plan with 10,000 credits a month. Paid plans from $6 a month as listed on the vendor page.

Best for: expressive narration, multilingual content and apps that need a voice API.

Murf AI positions itself as a studio for voiceovers. Its page lists more than 200 voices, built with permission and partnership from professional voice actors who earn royalties, and support for 35 or more languages for text to speech, with dubbing in 40 or more. The Studio editor offers pitch, speed and intonation controls and a custom pronunciation library, which helps with brand names and technical terms.

Murf also has an API. Its page describes Falcon 2 for conversational use with time-to-first-audio under 100 milliseconds, priced at $0.01 per minute, and Gen 2 for controllable voiceovers. Gen 2’s “Say it My Way” feature lets you record your own rendition so the model reflects your tone and inflections.

Pricing: Free plan with limits. Paid plan prices are on Murf’s pricing page.

Best for: marketing videos, training and presentations where you want to fine-tune delivery.

Speechify is built around reading aloud. You paste text or upload a PDF, DOCX, TXT or EPUB file, pick a voice, adjust playback speed and listen or download the audio. Its page lists more than 1,000 voices across 60 or more languages, including several regional English accents, and the tool works in the browser and in apps for iOS, Android, Mac and Windows, plus Chrome and Edge extensions.

The use cases lean toward productivity and accessibility: studying, going through emails and documents, language learning and support for people with visual impairments, dyslexia or ADHD. A free account saves your documents and syncs them across devices.

Pricing: You can start free. Paid plans are listed on Speechify’s pricing page.

Best for: students, professionals and anyone who wants to listen to documents and articles.

WellSaid Labs focuses on professional voiceover for businesses. Every voice is built from recordings of a real voice actor who consented and is paid when the voice is used, and the voices are licensed for commercial use. Its page describes hundreds of voices across languages, accents, tones and styles.

Pronunciation control is a highlight. You can highlight a word to see suggested pronunciations and save your choice to a team library that applies to every project, and set pacing, emphasis and pronunciation line by line. WellSaid also describes a Producer product that connects AI assistants to WellSaid through MCP and its API.

Pricing: Contact sales for a quote based on your voiceover volume.

Best for: corporate training, product marketing, courses and advertising where licensing and consistency matter.

Amazon Polly is Amazon Web Services’ text to speech service, and it is aimed squarely at developers. According to AWS, it supports more than 40 languages and language variants with over 100 male and female voices, and it works through APIs in your code. It supports SSML, the W3C standard markup for phrasing, emphasis and intonation, and custom lexicons that fix the pronunciation of acronyms and terms. Output formats include MP3 and OGG.

Pricing is usage-based. AWS lists a free tier for new accounts, with usage allowances that depend on the voice engine, so estimate your character volume before you decide. A short example shows how little code a basic request takes:

The sample uses the AWS SDK for JavaScript, calls the neural engine and sends SSML so that the pause and emphasis are explicit. Adjust the region, voice and engine to match what your account supports.

Pricing: Usage-based with a free tier for new accounts. See the AWS pricing page for current rates.

Best for: apps, IVR systems, notifications and any product that needs automated speech at scale.

Treat this table as a starting point. Features and limits change often, so test two or three tools with the same script.

Modern text-to-speech systems turn written words into audio through several stages.

Newer expressive systems go further by reading the whole script to infer emotion and context, and by accepting direction in the text itself, such as a bracketed note that says to whisper. That is why a single script can produce very different reads depending on the model and the instructions.

If you use a tool with SSML support, you can make a spoken code or number far clearer:

The say-as element tells the engine to read the number digit by digit, and the break and emphasis tags shape the rhythm. Supported tags and attributes differ between engines, so check the documentation for yours.

What is the best AI text to speech tool? It depends on the job. OpenArt suits voiceovers with video and music, ElevenLabs suits expressive multilingual audio, Murf AI suits studio-style control, Speechify suits listening, WellSaid Labs suits licensed corporate work and Amazon Polly suits developers.

Is AI text to speech free? Several tools offer free plans or credits, but limits are common. Examples include OpenArt’s free credits for new accounts, ElevenLabs’ free monthly credits and Murf’s limited free plan, which has no commercial licence.

Can I use AI voices commercially? Often yes on paid plans, but the rules differ by tool. Always check the current licence before publishing.

Can AI text to speech clone my voice? Some tools support it, including OpenArt and ElevenLabs, usually from a short recording of your own voice. Only clone voices you have permission to use.

What is SSML? Speech Synthesis Markup Language is a W3C standard that lets you control pauses, emphasis, pronunciation and pitch in synthetic speech. Amazon Polly is one service that supports it.

Which tool is best for developers? Amazon Polly and ElevenLabs both offer APIs, and Murf describes API options as well. Evaluate latency, languages, pricing and SDK support for your use case.

How do I make AI voices sound less robotic? Write conversationally, add pauses and emphasis, correct pronunciations and split long scripts into short sections. Choose a model that is designed for expressive reads.

AI text to speech is now good enough for real projects, but the right tool depends on what you are making. OpenArt is a strong first stop for expressive voiceovers alongside video and music, ElevenLabs offers a deep voice library and API, Murf AI and WellSaid Labs suit polished, controlled narration, Speechify turns documents into audio and Amazon Polly fits straight into developer workflows. Test two or three with your own script, check the licence and always listen to the full result before it goes live.
